sens: Accept as true what is told to us or what we see
Trust in someone, rely on them
Adhere to faith in God or the message of Christ
Hold something as certain, be convinced
Entrust something to someone
Be assured of the reality of something
G4100.detail:
1. The primary meaning is "to accept as true": to believe what we are told or what we see. Jesus says in John 8:45: "Because I tell the truth, you do not believe me" — the disciples refuse to accept his word as true. This is the contrast between truth and unbelief.

2. To believe also means "to have trust in" someone and rely on them for healing or help. The centurion in Matthew 8:13 believes that Jesus can heal his servant, and "at that very hour the servant was healed." It is an active trust that expects action.

3. In the Bible, to believe takes on a deep religious meaning: to wholeheartedly adhere to faith in God and Jesus Christ. This is what John 3:16 expresses: "Whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life." This goes far beyond mere intellectual acceptance.

4. To believe also means to be convinced, to hold something as certain. When Jesus asks, "Do you believe that I can do this?" in Matthew 9:28, he is asking if the disciples are convinced of his power.

5. The verb can also mean "to entrust": in Luke 16:11, Jesus asks, "If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?" — it is to hand something over to someone.

6. Finally, to believe expresses quiet assurance: Mark 11:24 says, "Believe that you have received it, and you will receive it" — an inner certainty of the heart.
G4100.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "to be stable, solid, reliable." In ancient Hebrew, אָמַן (aman) has this sense: to be firm, to be trustworthy, hence "to believe." Faith is not a light matter, but a solid support, something on which one can lean. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, this Hebrew verb is regularly translated by πιστεύω. The apparent noun, "faith" (πίστις, pistis), comes from the same root: it is the trust, the stable conviction of the heart.
G4100.emploi: This verb is one of the most important in the New Testament (about 218 occurrences). In the Gospels, it appears constantly: Jesus calls to believe in him and in his Father, to believe his words, to believe that he can heal. Mark and John in particular use it to express adherence to Christ. In Paul, to believe revolves around grace and justification: one believes in Jesus Christ for salvation (Romans 3:22). The meaning can vary according to grammatical construction: "to believe that" (+ clause) can express simple intellectual acceptance; "to believe in" or "to believe in" (with prepositions) expresses rather personal commitment, the trust of the heart. In Acts 19:2, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" shows that believing is a decisive event, linked to the gift of the Spirit. The verb is also used in the passive form ("to be believed") and with participles to designate "the believers" (Acts 2:44).
G4100.portee: To believe is not a simple opinion or calculation: it is to turn to God and to Jesus Christ with all one's heart, to rely entirely on him. For the Christian reading the Bible, this verb invites one to overcome the temptation of doubt and to accept the word of God as true and reliable. It is the fundamental call of the Gospel: to receive Jesus as Lord and Savior, not through a detached intellectual act, but through a living trust that transforms life. This faith brings salvation and eternal life (John 3:16).

sens: Of authentic quality, without mixture or adulteration
Trustworthy, faithful, and sincere
G4101.detail:
1. This word describes what is authentic and of premium quality, without dilution or imitation. In Mark 14:3 and John 12:3, it qualifies pure nard: a precious and true perfume, not mixed with less expensive substances, which explains its "great price."
2. Figuratively, it designates what is faithful, trustworthy, sincere — a person or thing in which one can have confidence. This nuance is especially found in non-biblical Greek authors, but it sheds light on how purity and authenticity go together: what is pure in its composition is also pure in its essence.
G4101.origine: The word comes from πίστις (pistis), which means "faith" and "trust." Pistikos, therefore, is what deserves trust, what one can "believe" — primarily because it is authentic and true. The basic image is that of authenticity that inspires trust: one can trust what is pure because it hides nothing, it is what it claims to be.
G4101.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallel accounts where Jesus is anointed with precious perfume: Mark 14:3 and John 12:3. In both cases, it qualifies the nard (a very expensive essence derived from an Eastern plant) emphasizing its authenticity and purity — which justifies its exceptional price and makes the woman's gesture even more generous. The adjective underscores that she did not buy a cheap imitation, but the true nard, the best.
G4101.portee: For the reader, this word reveals that the woman who anoints Jesus gives not only a lot but gives the best, the authentic. She does not hesitate at the expense. This detail of "pure" elevates her act: it is not a superficial gesture, but a sincere and precious offering, without economy or ulterior motive. This challenges us regarding the quality of our own devotion to Jesus.

sens: Trust in God or in Christ, an act of believing in their word and power
Set of doctrines, Christian truths that one believes
Faithfulness, the faithful character of someone
Commitment, promise kept
G4102G.detail:
1. Faith is primarily the act of trusting in God or Jesus Christ. It is believing in their word and relying on their power to act. A Roman centurion demonstrates this faith when he simply accepts Jesus' word without demanding to see him heal his servant (Matthew 8:10). Faith saves the one who possesses it, as the woman with the issue of blood touches Jesus' garment with confidence (Luke 8:48).
2. Faith also refers to the collection of Christian doctrines: what is collectively believed, the deposit of received truths. Paul speaks of those who "have turned away from the faith" (1 Timothy 6:21), or mentions that "the faith has increased" in the churches (Acts 16:5), in the sense of the body of doctrine and common conviction.
3. Faith can mean faithfulness or constancy: it is to remain steadfast, trustworthy. This nuance appears when Paul writes that "the faithfulness of God" does not disappear even if men are unfaithful (Romans 3:3).
4. Rarely, faith is a solid promise or commitment, like that made by a widow when she takes a pledge to Christ (1 Timothy 5:12).
G4102G.origine: The word comes from the verb "peitho" which means to persuade, to convince. Faith is therefore initially the state of one who has been persuaded, convinced. This is why faith is intimately linked to internal conviction and obedience. In Hebrew, it primarily translates the word "emounah" which comes from the root "aman" (to be firm, stable): hence the idea of a solid foundation, a sure support, mutual trust. Biblical faith is never a vague belief, but a heartfelt commitment based on the reliability of the one in whom one believes.
G4102G.emploi: The word "pistis" appears 223 times in the New Testament. It is primarily used by Paul and in the epistles, but also in the Gospels and Acts. In the Gospels, faith is linked to healing: Jesus heals according to the faith of the sick person or their relatives (Matthew 9:2, Mark 5:34, Luke 7:50). Paul explores faith in depth: it is the way of salvation by grace, not by works (Romans 4:5, Philippians 3:9); it comes from hearing the word (Romans 10:17); it is a gift of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9). As a virtue or doctrinal content, it appears in the pastoral epistles to designate the Christian message to be kept (1 Timothy 1:19, 2 Timothy 2:18). It can finally be accompanied by various prepositions (in, toward, on) to nuance the relationship to the object of trust.
G4102G.portee: Faith is the key to all relationships with God in the life of the Christian. It is neither a simple opinion nor an intellectual knowledge, but a confident surrender to the word and power of God. Where faith is lacking, God cannot act in power (Matthew 13:58 implicit). For the believer, understanding biblical faith frees from fear, self-justification, and vanity: it is standing on the unshakeable rock, not on the sand of one's own efforts. Finally, faith is never isolated; it is manifested through obedience, love, and perseverance.

sens: Trust or belief in God, in Christ, or in His promises
Faithful character, loyal, trustworthy
Personal commitment to remain faithful, solemn promise
G4102H.detail:
1. Trust or belief in God and in Christ is the most common meaning of the word πίστις in the New Testament. It is the act by which a believer fully relies on God and His Gospel. For example, in Mark 11:22, Jesus says: "Have faith in God," which means trusting in God's promises and power for our lives.
2. Faithfulness is the quality of one who remains constant and loyal, trustworthy. It is the moral virtue of keeping one's commitments and promises. Matthew 23:23 ranks faithfulness among the "more important things in the law," alongside justice and mercy.
3. The faithfulness of God Himself is unchanging: it does not depend on our unbelief, as Romans 3:3 states — "the faithfulness of God" persists even when men are unfaithful.
4. In the life of the believer, faithfulness is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), a virtue cultivated by the presence of God within, which enables one to remain constant in faith and commitments.
G4102H.origine: The word πίστις comes from the verb πείθω (peitho), which means "to persuade" or "to be persuaded." Thus, πίστις is primarily the state of being persuaded, the conviction that arises from persuasion. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), πίστις primarily translates the Hebrew אֱמוּנָה (émouna), which denotes faithfulness, loyalty, constancy — divine qualities par excellence. The Greek word thus encompasses two dimensions: that of personal conviction (believing that something is true) and that of loyal commitment (remaining faithful to the one in whom trust is placed).
G4102H.emploi: Πίστις appears more than a hundred times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles. It primarily denotes personal trust in God or in Christ: the act by which one accepts the Gospel and relies on Jesus for salvation. But the word also has an objective sense: "the faith" as a body of Christian doctrine, the collection of revealed truths (Galatians 1:23, 1 Timothy 4:1). A third sense emerges: moral faithfulness, personal loyalty. Matthew 23:23 makes it an ethical virtue that must be practiced; Romans 3:3 speaks of God's faithfulness in the face of human unfaithfulness; Galatians 5:22 lists it as a fruit of the Spirit. This richness of meaning shows that for Paul and for the entire New Testament, faith is never a simple intellectual belief: it is a commitment of the heart and the whole life.
G4102H.portee: Faithfulness, whether that of the believer towards God or that of God towards His children, is at the heart of the Christian life. It teaches us that authentic faith in Christ is not a vague or temporary feeling, but a lasting commitment, a permanent attachment that bears fruit in moral life. Understanding that God remains faithful even when we falter (Romans 3:3) gives us unshakeable assurance. Finally, cultivating faithfulness as a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22) calls us to become, too, reliable, constant, loyal in our words and actions.

sens: Who inspires trust, trustworthy
Who faithfully fulfills their task, reliable in their responsibilities
Who keeps their word and believes in God
Of a word, a promise: assured, certain, that will not change
Who believes, who has faith
Conforming to reality, truthful
G4103.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of someone or something in whom one can absolutely trust. God is faithful (1 Corinthians 1:9): we can count on Him without fear. The promise made to David is assured (Acts 13:34), meaning it can be relied upon.
2. In particular, faithful describes one who accomplishes their mission without failing. The faithful servant of Matthew 24:45 is one who does their duty toward those entrusted to them. A faithful person in little can be responsible for much (Luke 16:10).
3. Faithful also applies to one who truly believes in God and remains attached to Him. Abraham the believer (Galatians 3:9) and those who believe in God (1 Peter 1:21) bear this name: their trust in God is sincere and lasting.
4. A faithful word, a faithful statement is one that can be affirmed with certainty. "This is a trustworthy saying" (1 Timothy 1:15) introduces fundamental statements of faith that can be received without hesitation.
5. Sometimes, faithful simply designates one who believes, who has embraced the faith (Acts 10:45, 1 Timothy 4:12): it is a believer, as opposed to one who refuses to believe.
6. Applied to God or His nature, faithful can mean that He is truthful, conforming to His word, unshakeably true (1 John 1:9).
G4103.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to persuade, to make believe." Initially, it refers to one in whom trust is placed, one who persuades by their reliability. In Hebrew, the equivalent word (אָמַן) expresses the idea of firmness, solidity, certainty: something or someone unshakeable. It shares the same root as the word "amen," which means "let it be stable and true." Biblical faithfulness is thus a moral firmness, a reliable certainty.
G4103.emploi: This word is one of the most important in the New Testament: it appears 63 times. It primarily applies to people—servants, ministers, disciples—who fulfill their task toward God or toward men. It also applies, and this is crucial, to God Himself: God is faithful in His promises (1 Corinthians 1:9, 2 Timothy 2:13), He cannot deny His word. The word also designates things worthy of faith: a word, a statement, a promise that does not need to be verified because it is assured (1 Timothy 1:15). Finally, it can simply designate the believer, one who has faith: these trustworthy men and women in Christ (1 Timothy 4:12). The meaning oscillates between "trustworthy" and "who believes," but the text never doubts it: it is a word of strength and assurance.
G4103.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God is absolutely reliable: we can place all our hope in Him without fear. In return, He asks those who follow Him to be faithful in the small things, in the responsibilities He entrusts to them, for faithfulness is the cement of mutual trust. It is also a word of encouragement: a promise described as "trustworthy" in the Bible is not doubtful; it is based on the very nature of God who cannot disappoint.

sens: To be assured, convinced of the truth of something
To hold something as established, for sure
G4104.detail:
1. To be assured, convinced of the truth of something: it is to have the inner assurance that something is true and reliable. In 2 Timothy 3:14, Paul encourages Timothy to remain attached to the things he has learned and "recognized as certain"—that is, to those of which he has acquired a deep conviction, not by mere hearsay, but through personal experience and knowledge.
2. To hold something as established, for sure: it is to affirm something as true and unshakeable. The verb evokes the idea of giving weight and solidity to a conviction, making it reliable and trustworthy—just as one establishes a firm foundation.
G4104.origine: This verb comes from the adjective πιστός (pistos, "worthy of faith, reliable"), which designates what can be believed and relied upon. The verb literally means "to make worthy of faith." In Hebrew, it often translates אָמֵן (amen) in the passive form, expressing the idea of being assured or being held as certain. The family of the word revolves around trust and reliability: what is pistos deserves the faith placed in it.
G4104.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:14. Paul uses it to exhort Timothy to remain firm in the teachings received—not because an authority compels him, but because he has "recognized as certain," meaning he has acquired a personal conviction. The word suggests an assurance that comes from knowledge and experience, not from mere credulity. It expresses that deep certainty that only intimate acquaintance with the Word and those who live it can provide.
G4104.portee: This word invites the Christian not to settle for a superficial or inherited faith: it calls for a personal conviction, forged by study, prayer, and experience of grace. For Timothy as for us, it is about "recognizing as certain" the truths of Christ—not out of fear or conformity, but through an assurance that the Holy Spirit establishes in the heart of one who sincerely attaches to the Word.

sens: To leave the path, to get lost
To lead someone astray, to deceive them
To seduce, to divert from good
To err, to deviate from the truth
G4105.detail:
1. In the literal sense: a sheep that strays leaves the flock and gets lost (Matthew 18:12). It is the image of a creature that moves away from the one who keeps it, without protection or direction.

2. To deceive someone by making them believe what is false: it is to lead astray on a point of doctrine or knowledge (Matthew 22:29: "You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures").

3. To seduce, that is, to attract someone toward evil through cunning or deceptive promises, particularly by diverting them from God and the truth (Revelation 12:9: the devil "deceives the whole earth"). It is the action of one who deliberately abuses another.

4. To err or deviate: to live in confusion, far from truth and righteousness. Titus 3:3 describes those who were once "led astray, enslaved to various lusts," ignorant of God and the righteous life.
G4105.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of wandering (hence the French "errer"). In ancient Hebrew, the word תָּעָה (taah) carries the same meaning: to lose one's way, to stray. It is a simple verb that first describes a physical movement (to move away from the path) before taking on a moral sense (to deviate from truth, from God). The passive form shows that one can be led astray by another.
G4105.emploi: This verb appears 37 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, John, and Revelation. In the literal sense, it describes the sheep that get lost (Matthew 18:12-13). In the figurative and moral sense, it is the verb par excellence for speaking of spiritual deception: Jesus warns that false prophets and false Christs will come to "deceive" the elect (Matthew 24:4-5, 24). Satan "deceives the whole earth" (Revelation 12:9). But the word also applies to one who believes wrongly: disciples can be "in error" regarding doctrine (Matthew 22:29), and any believer risks "straying" if they do not walk in the truth (1 Peter 2:25: "you were like sheep going astray"). Revelation uses the word to describe eschatological deception, that of Satan bound who "leads astray" the nations (20:3, 8, 10).
G4105.portee: This word calls the reader to spiritual vigilance. It reminds us that deception is a real danger in matters of faith, not only from false prophets and seducers but also from the heart of one who can easily "stray." Jesus invites us to remain anchored in the truth so as not to be led astray. It is also a word of comfort: just as a straying sheep can be found by its shepherd, one who has gone astray can return to "the Shepherd and Overseer of [their] souls" (1 Peter 2:25).

sens: action of straying, deviating from one's path
moral or religious error
false doctrine or false belief
deception intended to mislead
illusion that causes abandonment of the truth
G4106.detail:
1. Originally, the word refers to the act of straying, losing one's way or direction — like a sheep that wanders away from the flock. It is a simple and striking image: the one who strays no longer knows where they are going.
2. In the Bible, this word takes on a very strong moral and religious meaning: it denotes the error of one who abandons the truth, particularly the truth of God. Romans 1:27 illustrates this well: men who reject natural law commit shameful acts and receive "the penalty they deserve for their error."
3. Straying can also refer to false doctrine, an erroneous belief. In Ephesians 4:14, Paul warns against those who lead us astray by "cunning" and "deceitful schemes" — misleading teachings that divert us from the truth.
4. Sometimes, the word denotes intentional deception: in Matthew 27:64, the accusation of "imposture" refers to the lie of the disciples who supposedly stole Jesus' body to claim a resurrection.
5. Straying can also be sent by God Himself as punishment: in 2 Thessalonians 2:11, God sends a "delusion" upon those who refuse to love the truth, so that they may believe the lie.
G4106.origine: The Greek word planē comes from a root that evokes the idea of drifting, wandering. Its primary meaning is physical — to lose oneself, to wander aimlessly — but the Bible applies it to the moral and religious realm: to stray spiritually is to distance oneself from God and His truth. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew "miramah" (Proverbs 14:8), which means cunning or deception.
G4106.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively to speak of religious and moral error or deviation. Paul uses it several times: in 1 Thessalonians 2:3, he asserts that his preaching has no foundation in error (unlike false apostles); in 2 Thessalonians 2:11 and Romans 1:27, straying is the consequence of rejecting God. Peter and John use it to describe false doctrines and false prophets who deceive believers (2 Peter 2:18, 3:17; 1 John 4:6; Jude 11). The meaning remains constant: straying is always a deviation from divine truth, whether moral, theological, or doctrinal.
G4106.portee: This word reminds the Christian that there is a real risk of straying spiritually — of turning away from the truth through ignorance, seduction, or disobedience. It highlights the vigilance that God requires of us against false doctrines and the seductions of the world. It also states that straying is never trivial: it has serious moral consequences and, without repentance, distances us from God. Finally, it invites the believer to earnestly seek the revealed truth in Christ, the only protection against straying.

sens: Going here and there without a fixed direction
Straying from the path or goal
Celestial body that changes position in the sky
G4107.detail:
1. The word primarily describes something that moves without order or stability: a star that seems to wander in the sky, unlike fixed stars. The ancients referred to planets, visible to the naked eye, that do not maintain a constant position among the constellations.
2. Figuratively, it qualifies one who wanders, who allows themselves to be diverted from their path or who strays. It is the image of a traveler without a goal or one who loses their way.
3. In Jude 1:13, the apostle speaks of "wandering stars" to designate false teachers: they shine like stars (they seem important), but they lack true direction, being driven like stars without a stable orbit, doomed to destruction.
G4107.origine: The word comes from the verb πλανάω (to lead astray, to deceive) which has the basic meaning of "to deviate." The "wandering" stars are those that do not stay in their place, unlike the "fixed" stars. In Hebrew, the parallel text of Hosea 9:17 uses נָדַד (nāḏaḏ), which also means "to flee, to wander, to disperse."
G4107.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:13. The apostle Jude denounces the false teachers who have infiltrated the churches: he compares them to "wandering stars." Just like a planet that moves without a fixed trajectory, these impostors are not reliable guides. The comparison is striking: they shine (attract attention) but deceive those who follow them. At the end of time, they will be plunged into eternal darkness, while true believers will remain stable in Christ.
G4107.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that some teachers may appear bright and important, but if they stray from the truth of the Gospel, they are "wandering": without foundation, without real direction, dangerous to follow. It is a warning to discern and to remain rooted in the word of God rather than being seduced by flattering words or ever-changing doctrines.

sens: One who leads astray, who deceives by leading to lies or error
Spirit or power that diverts from the truth of the Gospel
Person who falsely presents themselves to deceive and gain credibility
G4108.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone or something that leads astray: not physically, but morally and spiritually. It is the act of diverting from the right path through deception. In 1 Timothy 4:1, Paul speaks of "seducing spirits" that lead believers to abandon the faith: these are spiritual powers that seduce by presenting false doctrines as true.
2. On a personal level, a seducer is an impostor: someone who pretends to be what they are not to deceive others. The Roman authorities called Jesus an "impostor" (Matthew 27:63) — not that He was one, but to contest His authority and discredit His claim to resurrection. Paul admits to being called a "seducer" by those who did not understand him (2 Corinthians 6:8), while the antichrist is the ultimate "seducer" who denies the incarnation of Christ (2 John 1:7).
G4108.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "to wander, to stray, to deceive." It conveys the idea of someone who is lost or leads others astray. In Hebrew, the New Testament often translates this notion with the word meaning "fool" or "lost" — for one who seduces others acts foolishly against the truth. The Greek word encompasses both the action of leading astray (active sense) and the state of being led astray (passive sense).
G4108.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the Greek New Testament, always with a connotation of spiritual gravity. Matthew 27:63 places it on the lips of those who falsely accuse Jesus. In 1 Timothy 4:1, Paul applies it to deceiving spirits that emerge in the last days — an essential threat of the New Testament. In 2 Corinthians 6:8, Paul uses it ironically: he is treated as a seducer, but he remains faithful. In 2 John 1:7, the same term qualifies the antichrist himself, the one who refuses to confess the incarnation. Each context shows how lies can take on an appearance of truth and demands vigilance.
G4108.portee: For the Christian, this word is a warning. It reminds that spiritual seduction is real and current, not only at the level of false doctrines but also of the spirits that inspire them. The believer is called to discern error and to remain anchored in the revealed truth of Christ. It is a call to vigilance against religious impostors who promise what only the authentic Gospel offers.

sens: Flat surface and extent, made of stone or another material
Board or tablet used for writing or engraving
Figuratively: that which bears or preserves a truth, a message
G4109.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a flat and wide surface, like a stone table. This is the basic image of the Greek word: something flat and extended, without relief. In Hebrews 9:4, it refers to the "tables of the covenant," the two stone tablets inscribed with the Ten Commandments, kept in the ark.

2. More broadly, it is a flat surface intended to receive and preserve marks, writings, or lasting inscriptions. A tablet or board where one engraves or writes so that it remains. This meaning prevails in the biblical context.

3. Paul uses it figuratively in 2 Corinthians 3:3: the hearts of believers become a "table" on which the Spirit of God writes His law, not with ink on stone, but through spiritual transformation. This evokes the idea that a person, a heart, can become the living support of God's message.
G4109.origine: The Greek word πλάξ comes from a root meaning "flat, wide, extended." It regularly translates the Hebrew לוּחַ (loûakh), which refers to both the tablets of the tabernacle and the stone tablets of the Law. The same root appears in several Greek terms related to what is flat, flattened, or extended. It is a concrete word, rooted in a material image.
G4109.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul. In Hebrews 9:4 (or Hebrews, if the author is not Paul), it literally refers to the stone tablets containing the Ten Commandments, a major element of the tabernacle and the worship of the people of Israel. In 2 Corinthians 3:3, the same word is used figuratively: the hearts of believers replace the stone tablets as the place where God writes His will. Paul thus plays on the contrast between the Law engraved on stone (old covenant) and the Law written by the Spirit in hearts (new covenant). The word remains a strong term, evoking durability and gravity.
G4109.portee: This word reminds us that God's Law has long taken a material form on stone, a sign of its permanent and solemn character. But by placing it in the believer's heart, Paul reveals that God desires something more intimate: not an obedience imposed from the outside, but a transformation of the heart by His Spirit. The "table" changes from material and place, from dead stone to living heart. It is a word of hope for the believer: God wants to transform my inner self.

sens: That which has been shaped, molded by the hands of a craftsman
The created thing, in relation to its creator
Humanity or the creature dependent on God
G4110.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a shaped, molded object — like pottery or a statue from the hands of the potter. This is the concrete image of the word: something formed, with plasticity. In Romans 9:20, Paul speaks of the "clay vessel" that the potter has molded, which immediately evokes the idea of a material receiving its shape from the one who works it.
2. More broadly, the word applies to anything created and shaped — by extension, to the creature itself, viewed as the work of the one who formed it. The potter and his vessel illustrate the relationship between Creator and creature: one gives form, the other receives it.
3. In the context of Romans 9, Paul uses this word to remind man of his condition: you are a creation, a work of God, not His equal. It is a way of saying: you have no right to dispute with your Creator, as if a clay vessel could reproach the potter for its shape.
G4110.origine: The word comes from the verb πλάσσω ("to shape, to mold"), from the same root as our French "plasticité." It describes the action of giving shape to a material — hence its meaning of "shaped thing." In Romans 9:20, it translates the Hebrew יֵצֶר (yetser), which means "form" or "that which is formed," and also refers to the image of the potter shaping the clay, a central theme of biblical theology of creation.
G4110.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 9:20. Paul uses it in his argument about God's sovereignty and free will: he cites an imaginary objection from a man who would dispute with God, like a clay vessel criticizing the potter. This image is deliberate: by speaking of the "vessel" (plasma), Paul emphasizes the total dependence of the creature on its Creator, and the absurdity of one who dares to dispute with God. It is a rare word, chosen for its pedagogical strength.
G4110.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of a central truth: we are God's creatures, shaped by Him, and not our own masters. It is a call to humility before God and to trust in His wisdom, even when our paths seem inexplicable. For one who is going through suffering or confusion, this verse puts things in perspective: the potter knows what He is doing; the vessel can only submit to Him.

sens: To shape a material by giving it a form
To create, produce something by organizing it
To manufacture, construct through work
Figuratively: to constitute, establish
G4111.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of shaping a malleable material, like clay, by giving it a form. It is the image of the potter molding his material (Romans 9:20: "Will the clay vessel say to the one who formed it").
2. More broadly, to form means to create or produce something by organizing it and giving it structure. The emphasis is less on the material than on the creative act that results in an organized existence.
3. In a manufacturing context, the word evokes the action of building or producing an object through the work and intention of the creator.
4. Figuratively or theologically, to form can also mean to constitute or establish something: Adam was formed (1 Timothy 2:13), meaning created and constituted by God as the first man.
G4111.origine: The Greek verb plassō comes from a root expressing the idea of shaping, molding. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew yatzar (יָצַר), which carries the same image of the potter forming the clay. This image is very rich in the Bible: it evokes the sovereign control of the creator over what he shapes, and the radical inequality between the one who creates and the one who is created.
G4111.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, always in important theological contexts. In Romans 9:20, Paul uses it to describe the relationship between the potter and his creation: God, as sovereign creator, shapes His creation as the potter shapes the clay, which establishes the divine right to do what He wants with His creatures. In 1 Timothy 2:13, it describes the act of creation of Adam by God. In both cases, the verb affirms God's creative act and His absolute authority over what He has formed.
G4111.portee: This word reminds the Christian of a humbling yet comforting truth: like clay in the hands of the potter, we are created by God and depend entirely on Him. This should turn us away from rebellion against our creator and lead us to confidently submit ourselves into His hands. It is an invitation to accept our condition as creatures and to submit to the one who has formed us.

sens: shaped, molded
forged, invented from scratch
false, deceptive
G4112.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of something that has been shaped or molded, like a statue formed from raw material — a creation of human hands, constructed rather than natural.

2. Figuratively, it refers to what is forged, invented from scratch, without real foundation. It is false, artificial, a lie dressed as truth. In 2 Peter 2:3, Peter denounces false teachers who will exploit you "with deceptive words": they fabricate lying speeches to take advantage of you.

3. By extension, it qualifies what is inherently false and deceptive — not a sincere mistake, but a deliberate lie, a calculated ruse to deceive others.
G4112.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb πλάσσω (plassô), which means "to shape, mold, form." It is the same root used in Genesis 2:7 (in Greek) where God "forms" Adam from the dust. The word evokes the action of the craftsman who works the material — clay, wax, metal — to create a new shape. The basic image is thus that of molding, creative work; applied to words or ideas, it designates what is equally fabricated, but this time in a fraudulent manner.
G4112.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:3. Peter uses it to describe the deceptive words of the false teachers who have infiltrated the churches. These teachers disguise their lying teachings — their fabricated doctrines — as if they were biblical wisdom, in order to better exploit the faithful "for greed." The context shows that this is not honest error, but deliberate lying, manufactured words specifically designed to seduce and steal.
G4112.portee: This word reminds us that teaching lies is not a blunder or confusion: it is a fabrication, a product intentionally crafted to deceive. It invites us to vigilance: to ask God to discern between the true Word and the fabricated words that some present to us. It also reinforces our confidence: God knows His children and warns His Church of false teachers before they cause too much damage.

sens: The extent of something measured from side to side
The surface, the extent of an area or place
Figuratively, the breadth, the scope of a spiritual reality
G4114.detail:
1. Width is the dimension that measures something from side to side, perpendicular to length. This is how it is understood in Revelation 21:16, where the heavenly city has a length equal to its width: the same number of stadia in both directions.
2. By extension, the word can refer to the surface or extent of an entire territory. In Revelation 20:9, "the surface of the earth" evokes the entire expanse of the habitable world that the enemy armies traverse.
3. In a spiritual sense, in Ephesians 3:18, Paul speaks of "width" alongside length, depth, and height: he evokes the immensity and breadth of Christ's love, which cannot be measured in a single dimension but surpasses us on all sides.
G4114.origine: The Greek word platos comes from a root denoting the idea of extending or widening. It commonly translates the Hebrew rokhav from the Old Testament, which has the same concrete meaning: the space that extends from side to side. It is a fundamental spatial term in describing the dimensions of things and places.
G4114.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. In Revelation 21:16, it refers to a precise measurement: the city of God has equal proportions in all its dimensions. In Revelation 20:9, it designates the territorial extent of the earth. In Ephesians 3:18, Paul uses it in a listing of the spiritual dimensions of Christ's love — length, width, depth, height — to express that this love exceeds all measure and is grasped in a multidimensional way. The context thus shifts from the concrete to the spiritual.
G4114.portee: This word teaches us that spiritual realities are measured differently than those of the world. The love of Christ cannot be grasped in a single way, but according to its width, length, depth, and height — that is, in all its inexhaustible richness. For the Christian, it is an invitation to contemplate and experience the fullness of this love in all its aspects, and to understand that the heavenly city, whose proportions are perfect, reflects this order and absolute beauty.

sens: To make wider, increase the extent of something
To open further, increase capacity
To extend one's heart, become more benevolent and welcoming
To accept someone without reservation
G4115.detail:
1. In the literal sense, "to widen" means to make something wider or to increase its extent. Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for widening the fringes of their garments, these ritual ornaments (Matthew 23:5), to show their piety outwardly.

2. Figuratively, the word expresses the opening of the heart — that is, benevolence, moral generosity, and sincere affection. Paul tells the Corinthians: "Our heart has been widened" for you (2 Corinthians 6:11), meaning that his love and dedication toward them have intensified and expanded without limit.

3. The verb can also describe the attitude of one who responds to this love. Paul invites the Corinthians to "widen" themselves (2 Corinthians 6:13), meaning to respond generously to his affection, to be just as open and welcoming toward him.
G4115.origine: The word comes from the Greek "platus" (πλατύς), which means "wide" or "extended." In the Greek Old Testament, it mostly translates the Hebrew "rahab" and its derivatives, which express the idea of widening and expansion. The initial image is physical — enlarging a space — but it naturally transitions to the figurative sense of the heart opening with generosity.
G4115.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament. In Matthew 23:5, Jesus uses it in the literal sense to criticize the Pharisees. In 2 Corinthians 6:11 and 6:13, Paul uses it figuratively to describe the feelings of the heart. These three usages show how the same word can denote both a concrete physical action and the inner expansion of affection and welcome.
G4115.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that authentic faith is not external conformity, but a sincere opening of the heart. The widening of the heart is the sign of a true relationship with God and with others: it calls for generosity, lack of reservation, and reciprocity in Christian love.

sens: Wide and open way, public passage in a city or village
Open space where people gather, square or crossroads
Figuratively: the wide gate and easy path that lead to destruction
G4116.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a street or way in a city, that is, a public space where people circulate. It is the place where hypocrites liked to pray to be noticed (Matthew 6:5), where Jesus taught (Luke 13:26), and where the apostles healed the sick who were laid there (Acts 5:15).

2. The word also designates the squares or open spaces of a city, distinct from private homes. It is where the master sends his servant to gather the poor and the infirm for his feast (Luke 14:21), places of gathering and public life.

3. Figuratively, "wide" describes the spacious gate and easy path that lead to destruction: Jesus contrasts it with the narrow gate of salvation (Matthew 7:13). The image is that of a wide-open way, without obstacles, that many take.
G4116.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "to stretch" or "to be wide." It reflects the Hebrew רָחָב ("wide," "spacious"), which is mainly found in the Greek Old Testament to designate what is ample or extended. The Greek adjective πλατύς retains this idea of breadth and width, applied to a path or space.
G4116.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Luke, and in Revelation. It is used first in the literal sense to designate the streets and squares of cities where public life takes place: this is where people pray, teach, and heal. In Revelation 21:21, it describes the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem, made of pure gold. But in Matthew 7:13, Jesus uses the adjective "wide" applied to the gate and the path of destruction, creating a strong image by contrast with the narrow gate: what is spacious and easily accessible is not the way of salvation.
G4116.portee: This word reminds us that public life — our streets, our squares, our meetings — is the place where our faith is visible. What the hypocrites sought to show in the streets (their piety) was vanity; in contrast, Jesus taught and healed there. The image of the wide gate leading to destruction warns that the easy and popular path is not God's way: true faith requires entering through the narrow gate.

sens: action of braiding hair
woven or interlaced hair ornament
elaborate adornment intended for seduction
G4117.detail:
1. Braiding refers to the action of intertwining, that is, weaving strands or hair over each other in a regular manner — exactly like making a basket or a net. The word comes from the verb meaning "to weave, braid."
2. It also designates the result of this action: the interwoven hair that a woman arranges in this way. In 1 Timothy 2:9, Paul speaks of the "braids" that women may wear, and he advises against their use as adornment.
3. More broadly, it is a form of adornment or personal embellishment, often elaborate and costly: braided hair of gold or adorned with pearls, intended to attract attention and seduce through the richness of appearance.
G4117.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb πλέκω (plékô), which means "to braid, weave, intertwine." This verb evokes the image of strands or threads regularly intertwined — an ancient and universal manual craft. The noun πλέγμα designates what results from this weaving: a braid, a net, a basket. This image is found in many ancient and modern languages, as braiding is an art practiced since ancient times.
G4117.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 2:9. Paul lists what believing women should not seek as adornment: neither braids (braiding), nor gold, nor pearls, nor expensive clothes. The apostle contrasts these elaborate and costly ornaments with true beauty, which should come from modesty and the purity of the heart (v. 10: "what is proper for women who profess godliness"). This is a teaching on the priorities of the Christian life: inner testimony takes precedence over outward appearance.
G4117.portee: This passage invites the believer to reflect on their motivations when caring for their appearance. Paul does not condemn hygiene or beauty in itself, but warns against the seduction of ornament for ornament's sake — especially when it is the result of vanity or the pursuit of power and influence through appearance. For the Christian, true beauty springs from a life transformed by the Gospel, not from an investment in luxury or elaborate adornment.

sens: The majority, the largest number of people or things
The greater part, what clearly exceeds the others
Used adverbially: at most, at the very most
G4118.detail:
1. The word designates the majority of a group: more than half of the people or elements. Jesus reproaches the cities "in which most of his miracles had been performed" (Matthew 11:20) — that is, the largest number of his remarkable works. When Jesus enters Jerusalem, "most of the people in the crowd" spread their cloaks on his path (Matthew 21:8): the text speaks of the major mass that welcomes him this way.
2. The word can also qualify a reality as being "very large" or of first order. When Mark recounts that "a great crowd had gathered around him," Jesus gets into a boat (Mark 4:1), emphasizing the exceptional size of the gathering — the meaning shifts from quantitative to qualitative.
3. In 1 Corinthians 14:27, the expression "at most" limits a permission: "let two or three at most speak" — the word retains here the sense of maximum limit, used as an adverb to frame a number.
G4118.origine: The word πλεῖστος is the superlative of πολύς (many, numerous), which corresponds in Hebrew to רַב. This superlative expresses the idea of what is the most, the maximum on a scale. The root emphasizes the idea of abundance and considerable quantity — πλεῖστος takes up this image of "excessive," "which far exceeds the ordinary measure." It is a very common adjective in biblical Greek to speak of crowds, quantities, or degrees of intensity.
G4118.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Segond translations of the New Testament. It is mainly used in the sense of "the majority" to designate the majority of a crowd or a set: in Matthew 11:20 and 21:8, it qualifies the large number of cities and people. In Mark 4:1, it refers to a "great crowd" gathered near Jesus. In 1 Corinthians 14:27, it takes on an adverbial form to set a limit: "at most." The biblical context shows that the word is used to emphasize the extent of a phenomenon or to express a majority emphatically.
G4118.portee: This word reminds us that the Lord Jesus did not act in secret: most of the cities that received his miracles knew. This detail shows that the rejection of Jesus was not due to ignorance, but to the choice of the heart. In the Church, the word also helps us understand the importance of majorities and limits in the order of assemblies.

sens: Greater in quantity or number
Greater in intensity or degree
Greater in importance or value
More, in greater proportion
G4119.detail:
1. This word expresses superiority in quantity or number: "more than five hundred brothers" (1 Corinthians 15:6), "several years" (Acts 24:17). It is the comparative form of "many."

2. It indicates superiority in intensity or degree: the righteousness that "surpasses" that of the scribes (Matthew 5:20) means a greater, deeper righteousness. Or again: the widow gave "more" than the others, meaning a proportionally more generous share (Mark 12:43).

3. It designates what is superior in importance, authority, or value: Christ is "greater" than the temple or than Jonah (Matthew 12:41, 12:42). It conveys the notion of primacy and weight.

4. Adverbially, it means "more" or "to a greater extent": pressed to "speak of many things" (Luke 11:53), or the majority in a group: "most are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6).
G4119.origine: This word is the comparative of πολύς ("many, numerous"), very common in Greek. It naturally expresses the idea of exceeding a norm, going beyond. The root refers to the fundamental idea of "multitude" or "abundance." In Hebrew, it often translates the word רַב (rab), which denotes both a high number and greatness and importance.
G4119.emploi: This word appears 44 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and Acts. It is used to compare quantities ("several years," Acts 24:17), moral or spiritual qualities (Jesus' righteousness surpasses that of the Pharisees, Matthew 5:20), or people ("do you love me more?" John 21:15). Its meaning varies according to the context: it can denote a majority ("most"), absolute superiority (Jesus "greater" than the temple), or simply "more" in an action or state. It is a very flexible comparative term, suitable for many situations.
G4119.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize true greatness: not number or wealth, but the deep righteousness of the Kingdom, sincere love for God, and the primacy of Christ over all. It also calls for generosity without calculation: the poor widow gave more than the rich because her heart was more engaged. Finally, it emphasizes that faith depends less on the number of witnesses than on the value of their testimony.

sens: To interlace threads, strands, or stems by regularly crossing them to form a fabric or object
To imagine or create something by carefully composing it
To prepare or set up a humiliation or mockery
G4120.detail:
1. To weave means to interlace flexible elements — threads, straw strands, stems — by alternately passing them over one another to create a solid and unified object. This is the work of the weaver or basket maker. The three biblical uses of the word all pertain to the crown of thorns: the Roman soldiers "wove a crown of thorns" (Matthew 27:29, Mark 15:17, John 19:2) by intertwining thorny branches.
2. Figuratively, to weave can mean to prepare or construct something with intention, assembling elements to form a whole. Here, the soldiers do not merely pick the thorns: they actively work them to create an object of mockery towards Jesus.
G4120.origine: The Greek verb πλέκω comes from a root that evokes the action of twisting, bending, and interlacing. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses similar words like עָבַת (braid, weave) in Exodus 28:14, to describe the braided gold chains of the high priest's breastplate. The Greek word thus translates a concrete and manual action, well attested in the artisanal work of the ancient world.
G4120.emploi: The verb πλέκω appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Passion of Jesus: Matthew 27:29, Mark 15:17, and John 19:2. The three evangelists report the same event — the making of the crown of thorns — with the same verb. This terminological choice is not trivial: by using the verb "to weave," the evangelists emphasize that the soldiers intentionally worked on this crown, that they shaped it with their hands as a true work, revealing the malicious care and conscious awareness of their act of derision towards the King of the Jews.
G4120.portee: By reading that the soldiers "wove" a crown of thorns, the Christian measures the deliberate activity of humiliation inflicted on Jesus: it is not mere negligence or blind violence, but a thoughtful work of mockery. This verb invites contemplation of the depth of what Jesus voluntarily endured out of love, accepting that men composed his torment piece by piece, with intention.

sens: To exist, to be found in great quantity
To increase, to grow progressively
To have more than what is necessary, to have in surplus
To produce much, to bear much fruit
To exceed in quantity or intensity
G4121.detail:
1. To abound means that a thing exists in great quantity, that it is present in abundance. It is the opposite of lacking or being deficient. In Romans 5:20, Paul says that sin "abounded" before Christ came, meaning it was manifested everywhere and in great measure in the world.
2. The word also expresses an increase, a continuous growth. When something "abounds," it means that it is increasing, progressing further. In 1 Thessalonians 3:12, Paul prays that love among believers "increases" more and more.
3. To abound can also mean "to have more than enough," "to have in excess." In 2 Corinthians 8:15, the one who had "too much" did not lack — there was surplus for him.
4. For fruits and results, to abound means "to produce much" or "to bear fruit abundantly." In Philippians 4:17, Paul speaks of the fruit that "abounds" to the advantage of the Philippians: their gifts bear numerous fruits.
5. The word also carries a nuance of superiority: to abound in something means to have more or better than expected, to exceed the measure. In 2 Corinthians 4:15, grace "multiplies" and makes thanksgiving abound — the blessing exceeds what one would expect.
G4121.origine: The word comes from the root pleon (πλέον), which means "more" in Greek. It is from the same family as pleura (more) and pleôn (more complete). This root evokes the idea of what exceeds, of what goes beyond ordinary quantity. In Hebrew, this verb often translates words like "abound" (עֲדַף) or "multiply" (רָבָה), which have the same idea of growth and abundance. The verb perisseúô (περισσεύω), which also means "to abound," is very close but emphasizes more what exceeds the limit, the superfluous.
G4121.emploi: The verb pleonazô appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles. In Romans 5 and 6, Paul uses it to speak of the abundance of sin and grace: sin abounded, but grace surpassed this abundance. In 2 Corinthians, he describes how grace multiplies to increase thanksgivings and how the gifts of believers produce fruit abundantly. In 1 Thessalonians 3:12 and 2 Thessalonians 1:3, the verb takes a stronger active form: the Lord "increases" or "grows" love and faith among believers. In 2 Peter 1:8, Christian virtues must "abound" and grow in the believer. The context always shows a positive idea: the abundance of grace, love, fruit, virtue.
G4121.portee: This verb reminds the Christian that God's grace is never limited: it always exceeds sin, surpasses our expectations and merits. It also invites us to ask the Lord to increase in us love, faith, and virtues — not just once for all, but "more and more." Finally, it encourages us to see that our small offerings, our acts of faith produce abundant fruit that exceeds our sight, to the glory of God.

sens: Gaining an unfair or excessive advantage over someone
Taking personal gain by exploiting or deceiving others
Allowing someone else to gain an advantage over oneself
Using fraud or dishonesty in business
G4122.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to have an advantage over someone — not a fair or honest advantage, but one taken deliberately. It is to seek to gain more than what is equitable (2 Corinthians 7:2: "we have not profited from anyone").
2. This word primarily refers to the act of exploiting someone for personal gain: cheating, defrauding, scamming. Paul defends himself against having profited from the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 12:17-18).
3. It can also mean allowing someone to take an unfair advantage: "giving Satan the advantage" over us means allowing him to dominate us through his schemes (2 Corinthians 2:11).
4. In human relationships, it involves using fraud or greed: doing harm to others to enrich oneself (1 Thessalonians 4:6: "no one should wrong or take advantage of a brother").
G4122.origine: The word comes from the adjective "pleonektès" (one who has more), formed from "pleion" (more) and "ekho" (to have). The basic image is of someone who always wants to have more than their share — one who continually enlarges their territory or wealth at the expense of others. Insatiable greed is at the heart of the word.
G4122.emploi: This verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in Paul's epistles: four occurrences in 2 Corinthians (where the apostle defends himself against having exploited the faithful) and one in 1 Thessalonians. Paul uses it to warn against dishonesty in brotherly relationships and in the management of money. The word always carries a negative connotation: it refers to a morally reprehensible action. In 2 Corinthians 2:11, it means more like "to let win" in the sense of "to allow an advantage"; in the other passages, it clearly means to exploit or defraud.
G4122.portee: This word reminds the believer that absolute honesty should characterize their relationships, especially in money and business. "Light" dishonesty — profiting a little here, exaggerating there — harms brotherly trust and offends the Lord who takes vengeance. It is also a call to vigilance: not to allow oneself to be taken advantage of by one who seeks to exploit us, is to remain wise in the face of the schemes of deceit.

sens: one who always desires more, who is not satisfied with what they have
one who covets the possessions of others
one who is driven by love of money and possession
G4123.detail:
1. The greedy person is one animated by an insatiable desire to have more. It is not merely seeking to enrich oneself legitimately, but refusing to be content, always wanting more — more goods, more wealth, more possessions. In 1 Corinthians 5:10, Paul mentions the greedy alongside the immoral and the swindler, as someone whose disordered desires lead them to evil.
2. The greedy person is also one who covets what belongs to their neighbor, who looks at their goods with envy and desire for possession. It is avarice taken to mania: not simply loving money, but wanting it at all costs, to the detriment of justice and charity towards others.
3. Spiritually, Paul emphasizes that no greedy person will inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10 and Ephesians 5:5), for greed is a form of idolatry — it is placing wealth in the place of God. Money becomes their deity, and this exclusive desire for possession excludes the one who indulges in it from eternal life.
G4123.origine: The Greek word πλεονέκτης comes from two roots: πλέον (pleon), meaning "more," and ἔχω (echō), "to have, to possess." The literal image is therefore "one who wants to have more." The same root πλεονεξία (pleonexia) designates greed as a vice or disposition of the heart. It is a word that vividly depicts endless greed, always in search of surplus.
G4123.emploi: Paul uses this word four times in his epistles, always in lists of vices that exclude from the inheritance of the kingdom. In 1 Corinthians 5:10-11, he places the greedy in the category of serious sinners with whom a brother must not share meals — it is a matter of ecclesiastical communion and discipline. In 1 Corinthians 6:10, he directly states that the greedy will not inherit the kingdom of God. In Ephesians 5:5, he goes further: no greedy person has any inheritance in the kingdom, for greed is explicitly equivalent to idolatry. In every use, greed is treated not as a minor weakness, but as a radical obstacle to access to salvation.
G4123.portee: The entry reminds the Christian reader that endless material satisfaction is a major spiritual trap. Against the culture of consumption and "always more," Scripture points out that the love of money diverts the heart from its true destination: God and His kingdom. Recognizing a greedy tendency within oneself is an opportunity to repent and relearn gratitude for what one possesses, and generosity towards others.

sens: side of the human body, lateral part of the torso
wound or injury to the side
visible scar or mark on the side
G4125.detail:
1. The side refers to the flank, that is, the part of the body that extends from the arm to the hip. It is a fleshy area of the human body, clearly visible and accessible. When the angel wakes Peter in prison, he strikes him on the side to shake him awake (Acts 12:7).
2. The word also refers to the open wound on the side. At the cross, a soldier pierces the side of the resurrected Christ with his spear, and blood and water flow out (John 19:34). It is a concrete injury, an act of violence or completion.
3. After his resurrection, Jesus shows his disciples the marks of the passion engraved in his flesh: his pierced hands and his side (John 20:20). Thomas even insists on verifying this scar with his own hands to believe (John 20:25, 20:27). The side then becomes the visible and tangible sign of the suffering endured.
G4125.origine: The Greek word pleura comes from a root meaning the flank or side, a very ancient image of the human body. It often corresponds in translation to the Hebrew word צֵלָע (tsela), which also means side or rib. This vocabulary of the flank, the lateral side of the body, is universal and very concrete: it is a part of the body that is naturally recognized and touched.
G4125.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, exclusively in John and Acts. Four occurrences are in John 19-20, at the heart of the passion and resurrection narrative: the wound to the side inflicted on the dead Jesus (19:34), then the showing of the resurrected side as proof of the identity of the Resurrected (20:20, 20:25, 20:27). A fifth occurrence in Acts 12:7 uses it in the literal and physical sense: the angel wakes Peter by striking him on the side. In all cases, the word designates a concrete and visible bodily reality.
G4125.portee: The pierced side of Jesus is much more than a wound: it is the mark of his love and sacrifice. That Thomas can touch it, that the disciples can recognize it, makes the resurrection real and incarnate, not ghostly. For the believer, it is an invitation to move from unbelief to direct contact with the Resurrected: to see and touch in order to truly believe.

sens: To move on water aboard a ship or boat
To travel a maritime route towards a destination
To travel by sea with others
G4126.detail:
1. To navigate means to move on water aboard a boat. It is the action of the sailor or traveler crossing the seas. When the disciples navigate on the Sea of Galilee and Jesus falls asleep, this movement continues: the boat cuts through the waters (Luke 8:23).

2. The word also refers to making a journey by sea towards a destination. When Paul and his companions continue their journey by sailing past Cyprus to reach Syria, they are deliberately navigating in a direction (Acts 21:3). It is not just about moving, but about directing oneself.

3. To navigate can also evoke collective maritime travel: those who navigate together share the risks and hopes of the crossing (Acts 27:24). The centurion, the pilots, and the sailors each navigate in their role, but towards a common goal.
G4126.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that evokes movement on water. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew bôʾ ("to go, to come"), showing that it was used for any maritime movement. The family of the word includes several compounds: "to navigate towards," "to navigate out of," "to navigate through," which refine the idea of direction.
G4126.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament, concentrated in the accounts of maritime travel: the calm on the lake (Luke 8:23), Paul's three journeys to Syria and Italy (Acts 21:3, 27:2, 27:6, 27:24), and a prophetic vision on the judgment of Babylon (Revelation 18:17). The context is always that of the sea, the boat, and the crossing. Sometimes the verb is used alone ("they navigate"), sometimes with a preposition indicating direction or destination ("towards," "in the direction of"). In Acts 27, which recounts a shipwreck, navigating becomes the ordinary action that a storm disrupts.
G4126.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles and the early Christians had to face the sea to spread the Gospel. Paul navigated despite the dangers, and God protected him. For the reader, to navigate evokes both effort, risk, trust in the One who masters the storms, and obedience to a mission that requires leaving solid ground.

sens: Violent blow inflicted on someone
Injury or physical mark left by a blow
Suffering or punishment sent by God
Calamity, disaster that strikes a people or the whole world
G4127.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: a violent blow inflicted on someone. In the Gospel, the good Samaritan finds a man "beaten up" (Luke 10:30), that is, beaten by robbers. It is the blow of a whip or a stick that injures the body.

2. The word also refers to the injury itself, the physical trace of the blow. After being beaten in prison, Paul and Silas have their "wounds" washed by the jailer (Acts 16:33). It is the open wound that needs to be treated.

3. In a broader sense, a suffering or punishment that God sends to a man: he who sins "will be struck with many blows" (Luke 12:48), alluding to the consequences of divine judgment.

4. Finally, the word takes on a collective meaning: it is a calamity, a misfortune that falls upon a people or humanity. In Revelation, the "seven plagues" (Revelation 15:1) are the final disasters sent by God's wrath to punish the world before the coming of Christ.
G4127.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to strike": it is everything that results from a blow. In Hebrew, it translates words like "makkah" (blow) and "magga" (plague sent by God). The family of the word includes all terms related to violence and bodily suffering. It is a very physical image: we first see the arm that strikes, then the mark of the blow on the body.
G4127.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels and the Epistles (Luke, Acts, 2 Corinthians), it mainly speaks of real blows: whip blows in prison, physical injuries. But especially, the word is abundant in Revelation, where it takes on its meaning of divine calamity. The "seven plagues" of chapter 15 are the three plagues of verses 9:18 (fire, smoke, sulfur), the plagues that turn the waters into blood (16:3-4), the burning heat (16:8-9), darkness (16:10), and finally the giant hail (16:21). Each plague illustrates the power of God who judges the rebellious world. The term "deadly wound" of the beast (Revelation 13:3) uses the same word to describe a supernatural wound, healed against all odds.
G4127.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of two essential realities. First, that physical sufferings (blows, diseases) are real and affect even the disciples of Christ (Paul in prison), which should not surprise us. Secondly, that behind the history of the world stands God who judges and punishes: Revelation warns us that those who refuse to repent will be struck by his plagues. This is not a threat that paralyzes, but an urgent call to turn the heart towards God while there is still time.

sens: A large number of things or creatures
A large number of people gathered
The entirety of a group, the crowd considered as a whole
G4128.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a large quantity of things — fish, wood, sins. In John 21:6, after the miracle, the net is so loaded with the "great quantity" of fish that it can no longer be pulled in. This conveys the idea of a concrete, countable abundance.
2. It mainly applies to crowds of people who come to hear Jesus or gather for an event. In Luke 6:17, a "multitude" of people from Judea, Jerusalem, and the region of Tyre comes to listen to him to be healed. The word emphasizes the scale: there are so many that they cannot be counted precisely.
3. With the article, "the multitude" refers to the assembly itself, the crowd as a collective body that acts, decides, or divides. In Acts 23:7, when Paul speaks of resurrection, "the assembly" divides between Pharisees and Sadducees — it is the entire community, considered as a unit that can be divided or united.
G4128.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "filling" or "abundance." It translates in Greek the Hebrew "rob" (crowd, multitude) and "hamon" (noise of a crowd). The family of the word includes forms that express fullness, abundance, what overflows or fills a space. Thus, it is naturally the word for a quantity so great that it fills or overwhelms.
G4128.emploi: The word appears 32 times, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily describes the crowds that follow Jesus or seek him for healing (Mark 3:7, Luke 6:17, John 5:3). It also applies to quantities: fish (John 21:6), wood (Acts 28:3), sins (James 5:20). However, its major usage is in Acts, where it refers to the assembly of believers or the people: the twelve summon the multitude of disciples (Acts 6:2), the letter is delivered to the multitude gathered in Antioch (Acts 15:30), the assembly divides over the resurrection (Acts 23:7). The word expresses the reality of the gathered group, often in tension: a large crowd, powerful by its number, but also capable of confusion or division.
G4128.portee: This word invites the reader to measure the extent of God's action. The multitudes that follow Jesus show the scope of his ministry; the believers gathered in multitude express the strength of the emerging Church. But the multitude is also unstable: it can divide, be deceived, or act without discernment. This reminds the Christian that faith is not a matter of number or majority, but of truth — and that following Jesus alone, even against the crowd, can be the right path.

sens: to increase in number or quantity
to become more numerous (for a group of people)
to increase offspring or descendants
G4129.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to increase in number or quantity. When something is multiplied, there is more of it: the disciples multiply (Acts 6:7, 12:24), or God multiplies the seed of the sower and increases the fruits of his righteousness (2 Corinthians 9:10). It is a growth, an amplification.

2. Applied to a people or community, the word means that the group becomes more numerous. The Church grows through the assistance of the Holy Spirit (Acts 9:31), the people grew and multiplied in Egypt with Abraham (Acts 7:17). Each person added makes the whole grow.

3. The word also carries the biblical idea of offspring and blessing: God promises Abraham a multiplied descendants (Hebrews 6:14). To multiply then means to be fruitful, to see one's lineage grow, which was for the ancient Israelites a sign of divine blessing.
G4129.origine: The word comes from a Greek root (plēthys or plêthos) meaning "crowd, multitude, fullness." It is a causative verb: to multiply is to "make full, to cause to abound." In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew verb rabah ("to be numerous, to increase"), which expresses the prosperity and fertility granted by God. The biblical notion is rich: to multiply does not merely describe an arithmetic fact, but a blessing.
G4129.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the New Testament, primarily in Acts and the epistles of Paul and Peter. In Acts, it describes the spectacular growth of the Church: the number of disciples increases in Jerusalem (6:7, 12:24), the Church grows in Judea, Galilee, and Samaria (9:31). Paul uses it to speak of the spiritual harvest and righteousness (2 Corinthians 9:10). The epistles of Peter and Jude use it in greetings of blessing: "may grace and peace be multiplied to you" (1 Peter 1:2, 2 Peter 1:2, Jude 1:2). It is a word of encouragement and promise.
G4129.portee: This verb reminds the believer that the growth of the Church and the multiplication of spiritual fruits do not primarily depend on our human effort, but on the action of God and his Spirit. Blessing is not an abstraction: it is seen, it is counted. It also invites us to ask God to multiply his grace, peace, and righteousness in our lives and in the world.

sens: To cause a substance, material, or objects to enter a container or space until it is saturated
To fill a period of time until its end, to fulfill its duration
To cause to enter and invade the mind or heart with a feeling, emotion, or divine power
To accomplish, to bring to pass what was predicted or expected
G4130.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to pour or heap something into a container until it is full. In Luke 5:7, the disciples "fill" the two boats with fish to the point that they sink; in Matthew 22:10, the wedding hall is filled with guests.
2. For time: a period "fills" when it has elapsed, when the appointed days are completed. Luke 1:23 speaks of the days of service of Zechariah that "elapse"; Luke 2:6 and 2:21-22 speak of the time fulfilled before childbirth or circumcision.
3. The most frequent meaning in the New Testament: to be "filled" with the Holy Spirit or a strong emotion. This means that a power or feeling takes complete possession of the person, like water filling an empty vessel. Zechariah is "filled" with the Holy Spirit in Luke 1:67, Peter in Acts 4:8, and the disciples at Pentecost in Acts 2:4.
4. In a figurative sense, to "fulfill" a prophecy or God's plan: what must happen "fills up," comes to fruition. Luke 21:22 speaks of the fulfillment of all that is written.
G4130.origine: This verb comes from an ancient Greek root expressing the action of making full, of saturating. In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew מָלֵא (malé: to fill, to accomplish) and also שָׂבַע (saba: to satisfy). The word retains the concrete image of filling: one pours or heaps something until saturation, which explains why it naturally applies to the possession of the spirit by the Holy Spirit — a presence that completely invades the person.
G4130.emploi: The verb appears 24 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and Acts. In the Gospels, it first denotes concrete filling (boats, hall), or the fulfillment of passing time (days of service, gestation period). But its major usage concerns spiritual filling: being "filled with the Holy Spirit" occurs at least 16 times, almost always to describe a sudden ability to speak, prophesy, or act with divine authority (Luke 1:15, 41, 67; Acts 2:4, 4:8, 4:31, 13:9). In Acts particularly, this state of filling is that of the apostles and converts at the moment when God endows them with power and speech. The word can also express the grip of a negative emotion: anger "fills" hearts (Luke 4:28, 6:11; Acts 5:17, 13:45).
G4130.portee: For the believer, this word invites an understanding that the Holy Spirit is not a distant presence, but a reality that can "fill" our being entirely — our heart, our mind, our words. This requires "emptying" what usually fills us (fear, anger, doubt) to make room for God. It is also a call to obedience: to accomplish what God promises or commands is to allow his plan to "fill" through our lives.

sens: one who strikes, who fights
belligerent character, prone to blows
quarrelsome and aggressive man
G4131.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a man who strikes, who fights: someone aggressive who resolves conflicts through physical violence. In 1 Timothy 3:3, the Apostle Paul forbids an overseer from being "violent," meaning resorting to blows or aggression to dominate others.
2. More broadly, it describes a person's belligerent temperament: a character that seeks fights, who does not hesitate to fight to impose their will. In Titus 1:7, the requirement for an overseer is not to be violent, to control aggressive impulses.
3. Finally, it refers to a quarrelsome and aggressive man in general: one who terrorizes through threats and blows, who imposes respect through fear rather than moral authority. The word encompasses all forms of physical aggression or violent intimidation.
G4131.origine: The word comes from the verb "to strike" (πλήσσω). A plēktēs is literally "one who strikes." This root evokes the action of delivering blows, hence the idea of an aggressive and belligerent man. The word also appears in ancient Greek authors (Aristotle, Plutarch) with the same meaning: a man who resorts to physical violence.
G4131.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's epistles. In 1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 1:7, it is included in the lists of qualities that an overseer and deacon must possess—or rather, must not possess. Paul demands that a leader of a Christian community not be violent: he must be able to lead through wisdom, gentleness, and moral authority, not through intimidation or brutality. This is a striking contrast to the values of the Greco-Roman world, where physical strength was often admired. For Paul, violence is incompatible with serving God and leading a Church.
G4131.portee: This word reminds Christians that resorting to violence is unacceptable, especially for spiritual leaders. Self-control, indulgence, and the ability to resolve conflicts without striking or intimidating are essential marks of a Christian leader's character. It is an invitation to cultivate gentleness rather than domination through fear.

sens: Violent overflow of water that submerges land
Assault of waves against a structure
Trial that threatens to destroy
G4132.detail:
1. A flood is the violent overflow of a river or sea that invades and submerges the surrounding land. In the parable of Luke 6:48, it is a "torrent"—a surge of impetuous water—that strikes against the house built on the rock.

2. The word also evokes the repeated assault of waves against a structure: the image is that of a powerful force that strikes, tests, and threatens to destroy. The flood tests the solidity of the foundation.

3. Figuratively, the flood becomes the image of any major trial, any adversity that strikes forcefully against a person and threatens to annihilate them—hence its use to speak of troubles, misfortunes that overwhelm.
G4132.origine: The Greek word plēmmura comes from the verb plēthô ("to be full, to overflow"). It literally designates what is "full" and overflowing, hence the idea of a flow that spills out of its bed and invades. The root evokes the sudden and uncontrolled abundance of water. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word often translates terms like nāhār ("river, watercourse") when referring to a destructive flood.
G4132.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:48, in the famous parable of Jesus about the two houses. Jesus describes two men: one digs deep and lays his foundation on the rock; the other builds on the ground without a foundation. When the flood comes—the torrent that rushes against the house—the first dwelling withstands, while the second collapses. The flood represents the trials, the storms of life, the adversity that tests faith and the foundation of spiritual life.
G4132.portee: This parable teaches the believer that trials will come—the flood is not a hypothetical threat, but an inevitable reality. What matters is the foundation on which one builds their life: a faith rooted in Jesus Christ and His word withstands the assaults of adversity, while a life without foundation collapses. The word invites the Christian to examine the solidity of their spiritual edifice.

sens: Introduces a restriction or an exception to what precedes
Marks an opposition or contrast
Means "except," "excepted"
Links two ideas by providing a nuance or a turnaround
G4133.detail:
1. The word introduces an idea that limits, corrects, or contradicts what has just been expressed.
