For example, in Luke 10:20, Jesus says to His disciples: "do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven"—He rejects the first reason for rejoicing and proposes a better one. In Luke 18:8, "But when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?" creates a contrast: God will bring justice swiftly, but the question remains about the faith of men.

2. Sometimes the word simply marks a transition from one subject to another or a change of perspective without true disagreement. In Matthew 11:22, "why I tell you" renders the same word: it announces a conclusion that adds to the previous discourse.

3. Used as a preposition (followed by the genitive), the word means "except" or "excepted." In Acts 27:22, "there will be no loss except that of the ship" means "no loss except that of the ship." In Mark 12:32, "that there is no other than Him" = "none other except Him."

4. The word can also simply link two propositions where the second provides a restriction or an implicit condition: it is a flexible connector that allows the reader to sense the exact link between the two ideas.
G4133.origine: The word is formed from the root plē-, which evokes the idea of fullness or totality. In the Septuagint (the Greek Bible), πλήν often translates Hebrew words like רַק (raq, "only," "excepted"), בַּד (bad, "alone," "apart") and אַךְ (akh, "however," "only"). It is a very ancient adverb and preposition in Greek, attested in classical literature. It is used in everyday language to express fine logical nuances.
G4133.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke (15 times) and in Acts (6 times). It is primarily used as a conjunction introducing a restrictive or contrastive clause: "but" in the sense of "except that," "if not that." In Luke 23:28, "do not weep for me; but weep for yourselves and for your children," it creates a clear contrast. In Matthew 26:39, Jesus says: "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me! Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew translates a closer equivalence). The word is also used as a preposition (with the genitive) in the strict sense of "except" or "excepted": in Acts 8:1, "all were scattered... except the apostles." Sometimes it introduces a concession or a turnaround: "But" (= "However"). In all cases, it creates a logical pause and prompts the reader to reconsider the previous sentence in light of the one that follows.
G4133.portee: This small word teaches how God corrects or refines our thoughts: it does not always contradict our expectations, but imposes a relevant restriction or diversion. In Luke 10:20, Jesus uses this word to redirect His disciples' joy toward what is essential—not power over spirits, but the assurance of salvation. It is a word of divine pedagogy, showing how Scripture loves to nuance, clarify, and sometimes invert our first impressions to bring us back to the truth.

sens: Filled with material or object, to the point of overflowing
Completely filled with a moral or spiritual quality
Fully possessing a characteristic or virtue
G4134.detail:
1. The most concrete sense: a container or space filled to the brim. When Jesus multiplies the loaves, the disciples gather twelve baskets "full" of pieces (Matthew 14:20); it is overflowing. Or a head of grain whose kernel has become complete and ripe, ready to be harvested (Mark 4:28).
2. In a spiritual sense, it means being filled with a divine or moral reality: Stephen is "full of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:55), which means that the Spirit completely inhabits him and directs his actions. Similarly, one can be "full of faith" (Acts 6:5), or "full of grace and truth" like Christ in John 1:14.
3. This fullness can characterize a heart or a life entirely marked by a characteristic: "full of good works" (Acts 9:36) describes someone whose life overflows with charitable actions. It is a totality, a saturation.
G4134.origine: The word comes from an Indo-European root related to filling and abundance. In Hebrew, it primarily translates מָלֵא (malé), which means "to fill" or "to be full." The Greek family also includes "to fill" (πληρόω, plèroô) and "fullness" (πλήρωμα, plèrôma). The basic idea is one of a totality without lack, of a space or reality saturated.
G4134.emploi: The word appears sixteen times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and the Gospels. In Acts, it almost always denotes spiritual fullness: being "filled with the Holy Spirit" or "full of faith." In the Gospels, it first describes material abundance (full baskets, ripe grain), then progresses to spiritual meaning with John 1:14, where the incarnate Word is "full of grace and truth." The context determines whether we are talking about material (food, grain) or an invisible quality (faith, Spirit, goodness). The nuance of completeness remains everywhere: to be full is to leave nothing empty.
G4134.portee: This word reminds the believer that spiritual life is not a matter of surface or empty gestures. Being filled with the Holy Spirit or full of faith means being transformed from within, saturated with a divine reality that overflows in actions and presence. The contrast with "empty" or "hollow" invites us to seek this fullness: may our lives be "full" of what comes from God, and not of illusions or lies.

sens: To bring an action or project to completion, executing it fully
To completely fulfill a function or role to the end
To be fully convinced or persuaded of something
To be entirely filled with a disposition or feeling
G4135.detail:
1. To accomplish means to finish an action by bringing it to its complete end. The word implies a full realization, not a sketch: it is not enough to start; one must go all the way. In Luke 1:1, Luke speaks of the events that have "been accomplished" among us — the facts have truly occurred and been completed. In 2 Timothy 4:17, Paul says that preaching has been "accomplished" by him, meaning he has completed his mission of proclamation.
2. To fulfill a function means to carry it out by giving it its full measure. In 2 Timothy 4:5, Timothy must "fully discharge" his ministry — not doing it halfway, but with zeal and completeness. It is to give the full measure of the entrusted work.
3. To be fully convinced or persuaded means to have a certainty that fills the whole mind, leaving no room for doubt. In Romans 4:21, Abraham has the full "conviction" that God can fulfill His promise. In Romans 14:5, each person must have in their mind a full "conviction" on matters of conscience.
4. To be fully filled or to persist with assurance means to be totally committed in a direction. In Colossians 4:12, Christians are called to be "fully assured" and to "persist" in submission to God — the whole soul is oriented towards this obedience.
G4135.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek: "plèro-" (full, to fill) and "-phoreō" (to carry, to lead). Literally, it means "to carry to fullness" or "to bring to completion." The root "plèros" (full) appears in "plèrôma" (fullness) and "plèrôsis" (accomplishment). This word reflects the Hebrew idea of "mâlē'" (to fill, to accomplish), which implies an action that does not remain halfway but reaches its full measure.
G4135.emploi: This verb appears six times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles and in Luke. In Luke 1:1, it denotes the fulfillment of the historical facts of Jesus' life. In Paul's letters (Romans, Colossians, 2 Timothy), it takes on several nuances. It can express unwavering certainty (Romans 4:21 and 14:5), where it concerns the conviction of faith. It can also describe being filled with a disposition — in Colossians 4:12, being "fully" persuaded means that the persuasion fills the whole being. In 2 Timothy 4:5 and 4:17, it takes on a sense of active accomplishment: fulfilling a charge or completing a mission. The word always emphasizes the idea of a fullness achieved, of a completeness without reservation.
G4135.portee: This word invites the Christian to totality and sincerity. It is not about doing things halfway or with lukewarmness. Whether it is accomplishing the entrusted work, being convinced of God's promise, or persisting in obedience, the word demands a whole-hearted commitment. For every believer, it is a call not to settle for a weak faith or a service done out of habit, but to fully dedicate oneself to what one undertakes and believes.

sens: firm and unwavering conviction
certainty that fills the soul
complete confidence based on knowledge
inner security in the face of what might disturb
G4136.detail:
1. The word denotes a firm and unwavering conviction. It is the certainty that arises when one clearly recognizes the truth. In 1 Thessalonians 1:5, Paul says that the Gospel was proclaimed "with full persuasion": it was not vague words, but a proclamation carried by total conviction.
2. It is a certainty that fills the soul and determines it entirely. In Colossians 2:2, Paul wishes that believers have "full understanding" of the mystery of Christ: this means that their understanding is completely grasped and assured by divine knowledge.
3. Full assurance rests on solid and true knowledge. In Hebrews 6:11, we speak of "full hope": this is not a vague illusion, but the hope that is rooted in the promise of God recognized as true.
4. It is also an inner security, a heart confidence that dispels fears and doubts. Hebrews 10:22 invites to "draw near with a full assurance of faith": the believer approaches without hesitation, the heart firmly established on God.
G4136.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "full" (pleios) and "to carry" or "to accomplish" (phorein). The image is that of a capacity filled to the brim, carried to its accomplishment: one could say "complete performance" or "development without remainder." This fullness suggests not only the presence of a conviction but its total flourishing in the one who possesses it. The word belongs to the family of "pléroo" (to fill) from which "fullness" also comes.
G4136.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always to describe a certainty or a high level of spiritual assurance. Paul uses it in 1 Thessalonians 1:5 to qualify the proclamation of the Gospel itself: it is carried by full persuasion. In Colossians 2:2 and Hebrews 6:11, it applies to realities that the believer must possess: a complete understanding of the mystery of Christ, an unshakeable hope. Hebrews 10:22 uses it to invite to a faith without reservation. In each context, full assurance characterizes what is complete, without mixture of doubt or uncertainty: it is assurance brought to maturity.
G4136.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian torn between faith and doubt. It invites not to settle for a vague or timid belief but to seek this full assurance that transforms conviction into inner certainty. It is not arrogance or presumption, but the serene confidence of one who has grasped the truth of God and rests entirely upon it. It is a grace that God offers to those who persevere in knowledge and prayer.

sens: Fill a space or a container to overflowing
Bring to its end or limit
Fully realize an action, a mission, or a command
Implement, execute a word, a promise, or a will
Fulfill what a prophecy or Scripture had announced
Fill someone with a spiritual reality or emotion
G4137.detail:
1. Fill a space or a container to overflowing: the word describes the action of putting a substance into a container until it is completely full. For example, in Acts 2:2, the sound of the wind "filled the whole house" where the disciples were gathered.

2. Bring to its end or limit: to accomplish means to carry something through to the end, to the point where it concludes. When Mark 1:15 says, "the time is fulfilled," it means that the designated period has reached its final point and the moment to act has arrived.

3. Fully realize an action, a mission, or a command: to accomplish means to completely execute what has been ordered or what one must do. When Jesus says in Matthew 3:15 that he must fulfill "all righteousness," he means that he will fully meet all the duties and requirements of the law.

4. Implement, execute a word, a promise, or a will: to accomplish is to bring to action what was requested or promised. In Romans 13:8, "he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law": he has put into practice all that the law commands.

5. Fulfill what a prophecy or Scripture had announced: to accomplish means that what had been predicted actually occurs. Matthew 1:22 says that this "happened to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet" — the prophetic words are concretely realized in Jesus.

6. Fill someone with a spiritual reality or emotion: to accomplish can mean that someone becomes completely imbued with a divine reality or feeling. In Acts 13:52, the disciples "were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit" — these realities saturate them entirely.
G4137.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "full" and carries the image of filling a container to the point of overflowing. In Hebrew, the equivalent word is "malé" (to fill, to accomplish), which the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses for the same realities. The Greek word has gradually extended this concrete meaning to the broader sense of "bringing to completion" and "fully realizing": to accomplish an action is in some way to "fill" it until its complete fulfillment.
G4137.emploi: The verb appears about 88 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the Pauline epistles. In Matthew and Mark, it is primarily used to express that the prophecies of the Old Testament are fulfilled in Jesus and in his ministry (over 25 occurrences). In Paul, the word refers both to the execution of a command (Colossians 1:25) and the spiritual filling of the believer (Ephesians 3:19, Philippians 4:19). The context shows two main uses: on one hand, the prophetic fulfillment that proves Jesus is the Messiah (John 19:24), and on the other hand, the inner filling of the believer by the Holy Spirit and divine realities (Acts 13:52). The word also appears to express the fulfillment of the law (Romans 13:8) and the completeness of joy (John 15:11).
G4137.portee: For the Christian reader, this word is central to understanding that Jesus fulfills all of God's promises addressed in the Old Testament — it is proof that God's plan unfolds exactly as intended. It also shows that the believer's life consists of being progressively "filled" with the Holy Spirit and the presence of God, not by their own efforts alone, but by the divine grace that penetrates and transforms them from within. It is a word of assurance and hope: God keeps his promises, and he puts his Spirit in the heart of those who trust him.

sens: What completely fills, what is full
The totality of something, completeness
What is added to complete
The fulfillment, the realization of time
What constitutes the complete essence of a reality
The final perfection toward which God's plan tends
G4138.detail:
1. The most concrete sense: what fills a space or a container. Mark 6:43 speaks of the baskets "full" of pieces of bread — this is fullness in the sense of being filled to the brim. Matthew 9:16 mentions a "piece" of new cloth added to an old garment to complete it: this already conveys the idea of what is added to make full.
2. The totality, the complete whole of something. Romans 11:25 speaks of the "fullness" of the Gentiles who must enter into salvation — it is not a portion, it is completeness. 1 Corinthians 10:26 states that the earth "contains" all that exists, meaning it encompasses the whole.
3. What is added to perfect a whole: the missing contribution. Romans 13:10 sees love as the "fulfillment" of the law — what fully fills its meaning and scope.
4. The moment when a defined time comes to its end. Galatians 4:4 speaks of the coming of Christ "when" the times had been fulfilled — it is the instant when the duration is completely elapsed.
5. The totality of what constitutes the essence of a person or a reality. John 1:16 says that we have received from the "fullness" of Christ — it is the totality of his wealth, of his perfection. Colossians 2:9 affirms that in Christ dwells "bodily" all the fullness of deity — the complete set of divine perfections.
6. The state of perfection and totality that God wants to realize in his plan. Ephesians 1:10 speaks of the moment when "the times will be fulfilled" to gather all things in Christ — it is the final fullness of the history of salvation.
G4138.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "plèroô" (to fill). It primarily denotes the concrete result of an action of filling: what has been filled, what is full. In ancient Greek writings, it was used to refer to the complete crew of a ship or its cargo. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew "méloé" (what fills). The basic image is that of a container, a space, a time that is filled to the brim.
G4138.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and particularly in the prison epistles (Ephesians, Colossians). It has two levels of meaning that illuminate each other. At the concrete and everyday level: full baskets (Mark 6:43), a piece of cloth that completes a garment (Matthew 9:16). At the theological level: the fullness of Christ that fills us (John 1:16), the fullness of deity in him (Colossians 2:9), the fulfillment of times (Galatians 4:4, Ephesians 1:10). In the Pauline epistles, the word also denotes the fulfillment of the divine plan and the state of spiritual maturity toward which the Body of Christ is striving (Ephesians 4:13).
G4138.portee: This word shows that God never acts partially or halfway. Every divine action possesses a fullness — its totality, its completeness. For the believer, being filled with the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 3:19) is not a beautiful poetic image, it is a reality: accessing what truly fills, what is real, what is essential. It is also a promise: the history of the world is not chaos, it is moving toward fulfillment, toward this "fullness of times" where all will be gathered in Christ. Our spiritual life is therefore not in vain — it enters into this divine project of completeness and perfection.

sens: What is spatial: located near, in immediate proximity
The person who lives close to oneself, in the same place
Any person with whom one is in contact or relationship
One towards whom one has a duty of love and respect
G4139.detail:
1. In the spatial sense, the word designates what is physically close or neighboring: it conveys the idea of geographical proximity. In John 4:5, we see this literal proximity: the village of Sychar was 'near' the field that Jacob had given to Joseph.
2. It can also refer to the person living next to oneself, the neighbor, one who shares the same living space.
3. From there, the meaning broadens: the 'neighbor' becomes any person with whom we have dealings, we are in relationship, whether we encounter them regularly or occasionally. In Luke 10:29, the one who asks 'Who is my neighbor?' seeks to know: to whom exactly do I have duties?
4. But in the majority of biblical usages, the neighbor is one towards whom God commands love. The command 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (quoted in Matthew 5:43, 22:39, Mark 12:33, Romans 13:9, Galatians 5:14, James 2:8) transforms the meaning: the neighbor is no longer just the one who is near you, but the one you must love and respect as you respect yourself. It is an invitation to see in every person, whether stranger or familiar, someone worthy of love.
G4139.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning 'near' (πέλας). It translates the Hebrew רֵעַ (réa), which primarily means 'companion, comrade,' and more broadly 'neighbor, friend.' The basic idea is therefore proximity — both physical and relational. Transitioning from the Old Testament to the New, the word becomes a key term to speak of the mutual love obligation that God places at the heart of community life.
G4139.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in connection with the great commandment to love one's neighbor. It is omnipresent in moral teachings: Jesus cites it in Matthew 5:43 and 22:39 to recall the law of Moses; Mark 12:33 and Luke 10:27 report the same saying; Paul takes it up in Romans 13:9 and Galatians 5:14 to show that all love for the neighbor is summed up in this unique command. The parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29-36) illustrates who truly is the neighbor: not the one we choose, but the one who shows us mercy. Some usages are more scattered: John 4:5 uses the word simply for spatial proximity, Acts 7:27 uses it in a context of dispute between two men. Paul also urges the reader to do good to the neighbor (Romans 15:2, Ephesians 4:25).
G4139.portee: This word confronts us with a demand from Jesus that redefines who truly matters to us. To love the neighbor as oneself means rejecting selfishness and recognizing the dignity of every person. The parable of the Good Samaritan teaches us that the neighbor is not just the one we choose or who is sympathetic to us, but anyone in need of our help and compassion. It is a call that is both simple and demanding: to live according to love, not according to our preferences.

sens: Complete fulfillment, satiation
State of one who has received what they desired
Satisfaction of carnal desires
G4140.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a fulfillment that reaches saturation: it is like filling a vase to the brim. In Colossians 2:23, Paul speaks of 'the satisfaction of the flesh,' meaning the moment when the desires of the body are completely satisfied.
2. It is also the state of contentment that follows: when one has eaten to their fill, they experience satisfaction. Paul critiques here the religious practices that claim to master the flesh but, in reality, nourish and satisfy it.
3. Concretely, it is the satiation of carnal appetites — not only food but all bodily desires. The religious practice that Paul denounces (voluntary fasting, affected humility) ultimately satisfies the pride and selfishness of the practitioner instead of combating them.
G4140.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning 'to fill.' In Colossians, it translates the Hebrew idea of satiation (שָׂבֵעַ in Hebrew), which refers to the state of one who has fully received what they sought. The root evokes the action of filling a container until it overflows: hence the idea of complete saturation.
G4140.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Colossians 2:23. Paul uses it to criticize a false religious wisdom. The false teachers in Colossae imposed strict practices (food prohibitions, fasts, mortifications) claiming to combat carnal desires. But Paul denounces this illusion: these disciplines, far from mortifying the flesh, actually satisfy it, because they flatter the pride and self-love of the practitioner. They give an 'appearance of wisdom' but are 'of no value.'
G4140.portee: This word warns us against a very subtle spiritual temptation: believing that we can conquer the flesh by our own efforts and rules. Paul teaches us that human-imposed religious practices — even if they seem difficult and virtuous — often only satisfy our spiritual pride. True victory over carnal desires comes not from our efforts, but from the inner transformation that the Holy Spirit works in us through the grace of Christ.

sens: To hit someone or something
To reach, to touch violently
To inflict damage or suffering
To produce a sudden and visible effect
G4141.detail: 1. The primary meaning is physical: to strike means to hit, to harm something through a violent and direct action. In Revelation 8:12, the sun, moon, and stars are 'struck' by judgment: they are affected, impaired in their functioning. 2. The word also evokes the idea of touching, putting something out of normal operation. When a celestial body is struck, its light diminishes: this is a visible and immediate effect. 3. More broadly, to strike can mean to inflict a blow of fate, a plague, a judgment. This is why this verb is often used in Revelation to describe the plagues that fall upon the world. 4. The underlying image is that of a sudden and powerful action, which immediately produces its effects — an action that cannot be ignored.
G4141.origine: The Greek verb πλήσσω comes from an Indo-European root that expresses the idea of striking, hitting. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb נָכָה (naqah), which means properly 'to strike' or 'to wound.' This family of words in both languages always evokes a violent and direct action, like that of a blow struck by hand or weapon. The word belongs to an ancient warrior and judicial vocabulary.
G4141.emploi: The verb πλήσσω appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 8:12, in the passive form ('was struck'). The context is that of apocalyptic judgments: during the fourth trumpet, the celestial bodies are struck by the angel, and their light is diminished by a third. This verb is particularly suited to the visions of Revelation, which describe plagues and disasters. The passive form indicates that the celestial bodies are victims of a divine action, suffering the blow without choosing it — which emphasizes the power and certainty of divine judgment.
G4141.portee: This word reminds us that God is master of the elements and can intervene at any moment in the order of creation to execute His judgment. For the reader, 'to strike' reveals that the apocalyptic calamities are not chaos, but precise and effective acts of God. This invites us to take seriously the warning of the trumpets and to seek refuge in God rather than resist Him.

sens: small fishing or transport boat
craft used to cross a lake or sea
means of transport for the disciples with Jesus
G4142.detail: 1. The word refers to a small boat, more specifically a modest-sized fishing vessel. In Mark 3:9, Jesus asks his disciples to have a boat ready for him to retreat from the crowd pressing around him: it serves as a refuge and a practical tool for his ministry. 2. The boat is used to cross the waters (especially the Sea of Galilee) and transport people. In John 6:22-24, the crowd notices that only one boat was available, then observes that other boats arrive from Tiberias: these vessels allow Jesus and his disciples to move about, and they also serve the crowd in their search for him. 3. The boat becomes a symbol of journey and trust: in John 21:8, the disciples come with their boat full of fish, evoking the abundance of the miraculous catch. In all these passages, the boat is the concrete means by which Jesus' ministry is exercised on the waters.
G4142.origine: The Greek word is a diminutive of "ploion" (boat), formed with the suffix "-arion" which indicates smallness or affection. It is the quintessential small boat, one that can be handled without a large crew, suitable for lakes and short crossings. This diminutive reflects the reality of Galilee: modest fishing boats, not merchant ships.
G4142.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels of Mark and John. Mark uses it once to show how Jesus uses a boat as a refuge from the crowd (Mark 3:9). John employs it four times during the events of chapter 6 (the crossing after the feeding of the 5,000) and chapter 21 (the miraculous catch after the resurrection). In all cases, the boat is the setting for significant moments: the mastery of ministry in the face of the crowd, the journeys of Jesus with his disciples, and signs of power. The word emphasizes the concrete reality and intimacy of Jesus' movements with his group.
G4142.portee: The boat reminds the reader that Jesus' ministry is rooted in the real and daily lives of his disciples. It is in these small vessels that Jesus teaches, shows faithfulness to his apostles, and performs miracles. The boat also symbolizes refuge and shelter with Jesus in the face of the pressures of the world. For the Christian, it evokes the importance of staying close to Jesus, even in the ordinary and humble circumstances of life.

sens: small or medium-sized craft used to navigate on water
larger vessel capable of crossing seas
ship representing a dangerous or unstable situation
G4143.detail:
1. The boat primarily refers to a small or medium-sized craft, often a fishing boat: Jesus' disciples used boats on the Sea of Galilee for fishing, like James and John "who were in a boat with Zebedee, their father, mending their nets" (Matthew 4:21).
2. The word is also used for larger ships capable of crossing seas, particularly in the account of Paul's journey to Rome, where the ship is described precisely: "they used supports to undergird the ship" (Acts 27:17).
3. The boat becomes a biblical image of risk and instability, especially in storms: Jesus asleep in the boat tossed by the waves (Matthew 8:23-24) expresses the disciples' fear in the face of the elements, and the boat in Ecclesiastes (James 3:4) symbolizes something small that can be buffeted by powerful winds.
G4143.origine: The Greek word ploion comes from the verb plēō (to sail, to navigate). It generally translates the Hebrew onyiyah (vessel). The word primarily designates the object that floats and transports, rooted in the Mediterranean and Near Eastern experience of biblical peoples. Its root evokes the action of sailing, of moving on water.
G4143.emploi: The word appears 63 times, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. In the Gospels, the boat is the favored setting for the life of the disciples: Jesus teaches the crowd from it (Luke 5:3), calms a storm in it (Mark 4:37-39), walks on water (Matthew 14:29). In Acts, the vocabulary shifts: "ship" is more commonly used for the large merchant vessels that transport Paul across the Mediterranean (Acts 27), where the boat becomes a matter of survival during real storms. Elsewhere, the boat embodies a fragile reality in the face of powers (James 3:4, Revelation 8:9 18:19).
G4143.portee: The boat teaches the reader that Jesus masters the elements and protects his disciples amid storms. It also symbolizes the fragility of those who follow Jesus, but also their trust: being in the boat with the Lord means being safe even in the midst of danger. This motif invites the Christian not to fear adverse circumstances when they surrender to Jesus.

sens: voyage by sea
maritime crossing
act of navigating on water
G4144.detail:
1. Navigation refers to the journey by sea, that is, the route a ship takes while crossing waters. The word concretely evokes the movement of the boat from one port to another: Paul and his companions "completing our navigation" arrive from Tyre to Ptolemais (Acts 21:7).
2. It is also the act of navigating, the steering of the ship on the sea. When Paul warns his companions that "the navigation will not be without peril," he speaks of the risks associated with the crossing itself, the conditions of the sea, and the season (Acts 27:9-10).
G4144.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb πλέω (plēō: to sail, to navigate). Navigation literally denotes the action and result of navigating. It is a simple and concrete word that evokes the image of the ship sailing on the waves.
G4144.emploi: Navigation appears three times in the New Testament, exclusively in the accounts of Paul's journeys to Rome (Acts 21 and 27). In Acts 21:7, it simply refers to the crossing made. In Acts 27:9-10, the context becomes more dramatic: Paul warns his companions about the dangers of navigation at that time of year, as the fast (probably that of Yom Kippur, in the fall) marks the beginning of the bad season for Mediterranean navigation. The word thus emphasizes both the ordinary journey and the perils it entails.
G4144.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles did not travel in an abstract or miraculous way, but by taking the ordinary routes of ancient travel, with its very real risks. This shows how God uses human means — here navigation — to accomplish his plan, while preserving his servants amid dangers.

sens: who possesses a lot of goods, material wealth
who abounds in something (figurative sense)
G4145.detail:
1. A rich man is one who possesses great wealth, lands, gold, and abundant resources. Jesus encounters a rich young man who asks him how to obtain eternal life (Matthew 19:23); Zacchaeus, a rich man from Jericho, was the chief tax collector (Luke 19:2). This is an economic and social reality: the rich can give much to God, like those wealthy individuals who put large sums of money into the Temple treasury (Mark 12:41).

2. In a figurative sense, one can be rich in something immaterial: in mercy, in faith, in hope. God himself is "rich in mercy" (Ephesians 2:4): he abounds in compassion for us. The poor according to the world can be "rich in faith" (James 2:5), meaning abundant, full of trust in God. The church in Smyrna appeared materially poor but was "rich" spiritually (Revelation 2:9).
G4145.origine: The Greek word plousios comes from ploutos, which means wealth, abundance. It is related to the idea of fullness and abundance. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word ashir (עָשִׁיר), which means "one who has much," is regularly translated as plousios in the Greek version. This family of words always paints the picture of a person or reality that overflows, that possesses in abundance.
G4145.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the apostolic letters. Jesus often speaks of it while teaching about the spiritual danger of wealth: a rich young man cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, a camel cannot go through the eye of a needle more easily than a rich man can enter the kingdom of God (Matthew 19:23-24, Mark 10:25). Luke reports the parable of the rich fool who builds larger barns (Luke 12:16) and that of the rich man and Lazarus the poor (Luke 16:19-22). Paul uses it in a figurative sense: Christ, though rich, became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9). James warns the rich not to oppress the poor and urges them to humility (James 2:6, 5:1). Revelation uses it to describe the inhabitants of the earth who refuse to repent (Revelation 13:16).
G4145.portee: This word invites the reader to discernment. Material wealth is not inherently bad, but Jesus warns that attachment to money can divert one from the Kingdom of God. True wealth — that which lasts — is spiritual: faith, mercy, the love of God. A Christian may be materially poor but incredibly rich in Christ, or possess goods without serving God. This word prompts examination: where are my true riches?

sens: In large quantity, generously
In a rich and generous manner
With profusion and liberality
G4146.detail:
1. The word describes what happens or is given in large quantity, without stinginess. When the word of Christ dwells "abundantly" among the Colossians (Colossians 3:16), it is not reduced to a few scraps: it truly fills the community, nourishing teaching and prayer. It is the image of a wealth that overflows.
2. It also applies to the generosity of the one who gives. God gives us "abundantly" all things for us to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17): it is not a meager allocation, but a munificence. Likewise, the Holy Spirit has been poured out "abundantly" upon us (Titus 3:6), a sign of divine largesse.
3. Sometimes the word simply marks the fullness or fulfillment of a promise: entrance into the eternal kingdom will be granted to you "indeed" fully (2 Peter 1:11), with all its promised riches.
G4146.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek *ploutos* (wealth, fortune). It is an adverb derived from the adjective *plousios* (rich). It carries the idea of one who possesses much and makes generous use of it. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew words speaking of abundance and generosity.
G4146.emploi: The adverb appears four times in the New Testament, almost always to qualify the action of God or the divine word. In Colossians 3:16, it describes the generous presence of the word of Christ in community life. In 1 Timothy 6:17 and Titus 3:6, it emphasizes divine generosity: God gives abundantly (riches, Spirit). In 2 Peter 1:11, the word marks the full and complete fulfillment of a promise. The biblical usage emphasizes God's generosity, not human material wealth.
G4146.portee: This word reminds us that God never gives sparingly. He pours out His Spirit generously, abundantly provides for our needs, and offers us full access to the eternal kingdom. For the believer, it is an invitation to receive this spiritual wealth without fear and to live in the awareness of this overflowing divine generosity.

sens: To possess abundant goods, material wealth
To become rich, to enrich oneself
To have an abundance of a quality, a spiritual or moral good
To enjoy an overabundance of a resource or grace
G4147.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the possession of material goods in quantity. It is the state of one who has wealth, money, possessions. In Luke 1:53, the text speaks of the "rich" whom he has sent away empty: these are people who possess many earthly goods.

2. The verb can also express the transition to this state, the action of becoming rich or enriching oneself. In Revelation 18:15, the merchants who "enriched themselves" through trade with Babylon gained a great fortune through their transactions.

3. Often, the word goes beyond its material meaning to speak of spiritual or moral wealth: to have an abundance of a quality, a virtue, a good of the soul. In 1 Timothy 6:18, being "rich in good works" means to abound in good actions, to have a great quantity of them.

4. The word also designates the abundance of a grace or divine resource offered generously. In Romans 10:12, the Lord is "rich for all": He possesses and gives His grace without limit to anyone who calls upon Him.
G4147.origine: The verb comes from πλοῦτος, the Greek word for "wealth," which evokes the idea of abundance and possession. It is a verb that literally means "to have wealth" or "to possess in abundance." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb meaning "to become rich" or "to be rich." The family of words around πλοῦτος (wealth) is very rich itself: we also find πλούσιος (rich), πλουσίως (richly), and compounds like πλουτίζω (to enrich).
G4147.emploi: The verb appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul's epistles and in Revelation. It primarily describes material wealth: the rich in Luke 1:53, or the enrichment of merchants in Revelation 18:15. But the major usage is spiritual and figurative: Paul in 2 Corinthians 8:9 speaks of how the poverty of Christ enriches us, showing that true wealth is not temporal but spiritual. In 1 Timothy 6:18, being rich in good works is the goal of the Christian. Revelation also uses it for the false spiritual wealth of Laodicea (3:17-18), which believes it is rich while it is miserable in the eyes of Christ. The verb can convey the sense of a present condition ("to be rich") or a transition ("to become rich").
G4147.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the true meaning of wealth: it is not in earthly possessions, but in the grace of God and in works of righteousness. Christ became poor so that we might be spiritually enriched — this is the wonderful exchange of the Gospel. For the Christian, being "rich" means abounding in good works, generosity, and faith, rather than accumulating money. It is a word of freedom for those who fear lacking.

sens: Make rich, increase someone's material wealth
Fill with abundance, fullness
Enrich spiritually, provide immaterial goods such as knowledge or grace
Prosper someone through generosity and sharing
G4148.detail:
1. The basic meaning is to make someone rich in a material sense — to give or increase their possessions. It is the image of the word: moving from poverty to abundance.

2. The verb can also mean to fill someone with fullness and abundance in all things, overflowing with generosity towards them. In 1 Corinthians 1:5, believers are "enriched in all speech" spiritually in Christ.

3. Very often in the New Testament, enriching becomes a spiritual act: giving someone goods that are not money, but of the spirit — knowledge, grace, God's gifts. It is enriching the soul, faith, inner life.

4. The word also evokes the prosperity that comes from generous acts: in 2 Corinthians 6:10, Paul says that by giving himself to others despite his poverty, he "enriches many." It is the idea that offering one's life and love enriches those who receive it.
G4148.origine: The verb comes from the Greek noun πλοῦτος (ploutos), which means wealth, fortune, abundance. The root evokes the idea of filling, completing. In ancient Hebrew, the verb עָשַׁר (ashar, which the Greek Old Testament often translates with this word) also means to become rich or to enrich. The Greek word is constructed with an object complement (the person being enriched) and describes the action of pouring abundance upon someone with wealth, whether material or spiritual.
G4148.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Paul, and almost always in the passive voice ("to be enriched"). In 1 Corinthians 1:5, Paul thanks God because the Corinthians have been enriched in Christ with all speech and knowledge — a spiritual wealth. In 2 Corinthians 6:10, Paul states a Pauline paradox: although poor in the eyes of the world, he enriches many people through his ministry and faith. In 2 Corinthians 9:11, enrichment is the fruit of generosity: give freely, and you will be enriched in every way so that you can be generous on every occasion. The word is always linked to God's grace or the beneficial consequence of a life given.
G4148.portee: This verb shows a profound truth: true wealth is not money, but the knowledge of God, His grace, and the ability to bless others. By giving generously, one does not become poor; one becomes rich, enriched by God Himself. It is a call not to fear material poverty when walking with Christ, for spiritual goods infinitely surpass earthly riches.

sens: Material goods, money, possessions
Abundance of something precious
Generosity, generous gift
Splendor, glory, divine excellence
G4149.detail:
1. Wealth primarily refers to material goods and money: earthly possessions that can seduce us and lead us away from God. In Matthew 13:22, Jesus speaks of one who "the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke" the Word. This is the most concrete meaning, that of treasures and visible prosperity.

2. The word also describes the abundance or fullness of a precious quality: the richness of God's goodness (Romans 2:4), the richness of His wisdom (Romans 11:33). It is an inner treasure, an inexhaustible depth.

3. Wealth can signify generosity, the liberal outpouring of what one possesses. The Corinthians, despite their poverty, give "according to their ability" and "beyond" (2 Corinthians 8:2), demonstrating a richness of heart.

4. Finally, the word evokes splendor and glory: the riches of the glory of the inheritance that God reserves for the saints (Ephesians 1:18), or that which He strengthens the inner man with (Ephesians 3:16). It is heavenly wealth, inexhaustible and eternal.
G4149.origine: The Greek word ploutos comes from a root meaning abundance and fullness. In Hebrew, it translates the word עֹשֶׁר (osher), which carries the same idea: wealth as an accumulation of goods and, figuratively, as an abundance of qualities or gifts. The word belongs to a Greek family that speaks of filling and fullness, hence its use for both money and spiritual gifts.
G4149.emploi: The word "wealth" appears 21 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels and practical epistles (Matthew, Mark, Luke, 1 Timothy, James), it often refers to material wealth and its traps: the seduction of earthly goods that choke the Word or tempt believers. But especially in Paul, it changes meaning: he speaks of the wealth of God — His goodness, wisdom, grace, glory. This spiritual wealth is inexhaustible and is liberally distributed to believers (Ephesians 1:18, 3:16, Colossians 2:2). It is the transition from a wealth that possesses us to a wealth that we possess in truth.
G4149.portee: This word compels us to discern: material wealth can seduce and lead us away from God, but true wealth is that of God — His goodness, wisdom, glory. It impoverishes no one and does not wear out. The believer is called to "be enriched" by God's gifts rather than pursue perishable treasures. It is an invitation to overturn our values and recognize that generosity — sharing what we possess — is a form of wealth far more precious.

sens: clean with water (objects, clothing)
purify, make white (in a spiritual sense)
G4150.detail:
1. To wash means to clean something with water. It is the concrete act of washing: in Luke 5:2, the fishermen wash their nets after a night of fishing to clean and prepare them. The word particularly applies to clothing and material objects.
2. Figuratively and spiritually, to wash refers to the purification of the soul and guilt. In Revelation 7:14, those who have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb represent believers purified from their sins by Christ's sacrifice. Similarly, in Revelation 22:14, washing one's robes means to spiritually purify oneself to gain access to eternal life and the city of God.
G4150.origine: The verb πλύνω comes from a Greek root that denotes the action of rubbing and cleaning. In Hebrew, it primarily corresponds to כָּבַס (kābas), the classic word for washing clothes and fabrics. This image of washing with water, which makes white and pure, has naturally taken on a moral and spiritual significance in the Bible: to wash is also to purify from the stain of sin.
G4150.emploi: The verb πλύνω appears three times in the New Testament, always in these two contexts: material washing and spiritual purification. In Luke 5:2, it describes the daily work of fishermen washing their nets. But the two occurrences in Revelation reveal the depth of the word: washing one's robes in the blood of the Lamb becomes the central metaphor of redemption. This progression shows how an ordinary word becomes laden with theological meaning: from the physical act of cleaning to the spiritual reality of purification in Christ.
G4150.portee: For the believer, the word "wash" reminds us that the purification of sin is not a mere abstraction: it is concrete, real, like a washing that removes dirt. It is by the blood of the Lamb, through Christ's sacrifice, that our sins are erased and we become white as snow. This image invites us to take seriously the reality of our guilt and the transformative power of God's grace.

sens: Breath or wind, moving air
Vital principle that animates a living being
Inner disposition, state of soul, intention
Incorporeal being, creature without flesh: angel, demon, or soul of the deceased
Personal divine power: the Holy Spirit, gift and action of God
Self considered in its deep reality, the interiority
G4151G.detail:
1. The breath of air, the wind: this is the most concrete meaning of the Greek word. In John 3:8, Jesus says, "the wind (pneuma) blows where it wishes," using the image of the wind to speak of spiritual realities that we cannot control.
2. The principle of life that animates the body: that which breathes, that which lives. When Jesus breathes his last on the cross (Luke 23:46), he commits his spirit, meaning his life. In Luke 8:55, the spirit returns to Jairus' daughter, bringing her back to life.
3. The inner state of someone, their attitude, their heart's intention: for example, a spirit of wisdom, love, or fear. In 2 Timothy 1:7, Paul speaks of "the spirit of fear" opposed to a spirit of power and love.
4. A personal being without a body: an angel, a demon, or the soul of a deceased person. In Luke 24:37, the apostles think they see a ghost (spirit); in Acts 16:16, the possessed girl has a spirit of Python, meaning a demon that spoke through her.
5. The Holy Spirit, the power and presence of God in person, whom he sends to invigorate, guide, and transform believers. This is the most important and frequent meaning: in Matthew 3:16, at Jesus' baptism, the Spirit of God descends upon him.
6. Self in its inner and spiritual reality, not just one's body or rational thoughts: in 1 Corinthians 5:3, Paul says he is present "in spirit" even though absent in body, meaning that his deep being is engaged.
G4151G.origine: The Greek word pneuma comes from a root that means "to blow" or "to breathe." In classical Greek literature, it refers to vital breath, respiration. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates the word ruah, which means both wind, breath of life, and the Spirit of God. The writers of the New Testament, speaking Greek to Jews or using the Greek text of the Old Testament, naturally use this word to evoke the spiritual reality that the Hebrews called ruah: the living and supernatural action of God.
G4151G.emploi: The word pneuma appears more than 340 times in the New Testament; it is one of the most important words. It first denotes wind and breath (John 3:8), then very often the Holy Spirit: in the Gospels, during significant moments (baptism, temptation, resurrection), in Acts where it guides the Church and fills believers, in Paul's letters where he speaks of living "according to the Spirit" and not "according to the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). The word is also used for spiritual creatures, the evil spirits that Jesus casts out (Matthew 8:16, Mark 1:23), and the souls of the righteous after death (Hebrews 12:23). Depending on the context and the presence or absence of the article, the same word can mean the temporary action of the Holy Spirit or his stable personal presence. The richness of the word reflects the biblical conviction that the invisible spiritual is as real as the visible material.
G4151G.portee: For the Christian faith, understanding this word is crucial: Jesus teaches that the wind represents the mysterious action of the Holy Spirit, which is unseen but whose effects can be seen (John 3:8). Recognizing the Holy Spirit as a personal and benevolent power of God transforms the believer's prayer, trust, and obedience. Distinguishing between the spirit (the inner being) and the flesh (selfish impulses) helps to understand the spiritual struggle and the inner transformation that Christ brings about. Finally, the certainty that there are invisible spiritual realities (God, angels, demons) underpins the entire life of faith beyond materialism.

sens: Wind or movement of air
Breath, respiration
Vital principle that animates a body
Incorporeal being, immaterial person
Inner disposition, state of soul
Holy Spirit, presence and power of God
G4151H.detail:
1. The wind that blows: this is the movement of air that can be heard but not seen (John 3:8, "The wind blows where it wishes"). Jesus uses this image to speak of the Holy Spirit, who acts freely and mysteriously.
2. The breath of the mouth: the air that comes out of respiration, or metaphorically the powerful word (2 Thessalonians 2:8, "by the breath of his mouth"). It is a force that comes from the one who speaks.
3. That which gives life to a body: the hidden principle that gives life and animation to matter. This is why Revelation 11:11 speaks of a "spirit of life" entering witnesses to resurrect them.
4. An immaterial being, an invisible presence: an angel, a demon, or the soul of a deceased person. It is a person or a power without a physical body.
5. The inner state, the attitude or influence that governs us: a spirit of fear, wisdom, or goodness. It is what drives someone to act or think in a certain way.
6. The Holy Spirit of God: the divine presence and power that dwells in the believer's heart and transforms them. It is God himself acting in us.
G4151H.origine: The Greek word pneuma comes from the root that means "to blow" and primarily refers to moving air, the wind that we cannot see but can feel. The Hebrew Bible uses the word ruah (רוּחַ) in the same way: it is primarily the wind, but also breath, respiration, and by extension the whole being, inner life, and the Spirit of God. The Greek word has retained this richness and ambiguity: a term that designates both a material reality (moving air) and immaterial realities (the soul, the divine presence). This progression from the tangible to the intangible is at the very heart of the word.
G4151H.emploi: The word appears about 380 times in the New Testament. It first covers concrete meanings: natural wind (John 3:8), the breath that comes from the mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8). It then denotes the invisible vital principle, the soul or immaterial essence of a living being (Revelation 11:11). It also speaks of spiritual beings: evil spirits (demons) that are frequently encountered in exorcism accounts (Luke 4:33, Acts 19:12), and angels (Hebrews 1:14). But its major usage pertains to the Holy Spirit: the presence of God that fills, sanctifies, inspires, and governs believers. It is the key word for speaking about the spiritual life of the Christian and the action of God in us.
G4151H.portee: Understanding this word means grasping that the invisible reality — God, spirits, our own inner life — is as true and powerful as what we see. It also reminds us that the word comes from a wind and a breath: the Holy Spirit is not a theory, but a living, free, and transformative presence that seizes us. For the believer, the Spirit is not an impersonal force, but the Spirit of God who gives new life, leads to truth, and unites all believers into one body.

sens: Belonging to the Spirit of God or animated by it
Concerning the human spirit, as opposed to the body or carnal desires
Originating from the Spirit of God and not from human wisdom
Relating to life with God, as opposed to temporal and material things
G4152.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning refers to what belongs to the Spirit of God or what is produced by Him. A "spiritual" person is one governed by the Spirit of God and capable of discerning the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:15). "Spiritual blessings" are those that God gives through His Spirit (Ephesians 1:3).
2. The word contrasts with "animal" or "carnal": it designates what belongs to the spirit, to the inner life, in relation to the body or natural instincts. A "spiritual body" at the resurrection is not an ordinary physical body, but a body transformed by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:44).
3. "Spiritual things" are those that come from the Spirit and not from mere human intelligence: the Word of God taught by the Spirit is received in a "spiritual" language, that is, in accordance with divine reality (1 Corinthians 2:13).
4. It also contrasts with the temporal and material: "spiritual goods" (the Gospel, life in Christ) are distinguished from "temporal goods" (money, food), to show that what comes from God infinitely surpasses what is purely earthly (1 Corinthians 9:11).
G4152.origine: The word comes from the Greek "pneuma" which means "breath," "respiration," or "spirit." Originally, the word described what was related to air or wind. In biblical thought, it has taken on the meaning of what belongs to the Spirit—the Spirit of God who is the divine breath of life. The adjective "spiritual" thus qualifies everything that is animated, governed, or produced by this divine Spirit, as opposed to what is merely physical, material, or governed by the flesh.
G4152.emploi: The word "spiritual" appears about 21 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul’s writings. It characterizes the gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:1), mature believers (1 Corinthians 2:15; 3:1), the food or blessings that God grants (1 Corinthians 10:3-4; Ephesians 1:3), and the Christian's struggles (Ephesians 6:12). Paul uses it to distinguish what comes from the Spirit of God from what comes from mere human reason, the flesh, or the world. Its usage varies according to context: it can qualify people (a spiritual person discerns the things of God), gifts (spiritual gifts), or invisible realities (spiritual blessings, spiritual warfare).
G4152.portee: Understanding what it means to be "spiritual" helps the Christian to orient their life. It is not a state reserved for a few chosen ones, but the result of allowing the Spirit of God to govern one's thoughts and actions. Recognizing "spiritual goods" as superior to temporal goods puts true priorities into perspective: a living relationship with God is worth infinitely more than money or possessions. Finally, viewing the Christian struggle as a "spiritual" battle invites one to seek the weapons and resources that only the Spirit can provide, not carnal strategies.

sens: With the help of the Holy Spirit, in a manner consistent with the Spirit of God
As a spiritual reality, beyond the literal sense
G4153.detail:
1. The word designates the way of discerning and understanding things that come from God through the Holy Spirit. In 1 Corinthians 2:14, Paul explains that the natural man (the one who does not receive faith) cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God because they are spiritually discerned—that is, one needs the illumination of the Holy Spirit to grasp them.
2. The word also means: in a spiritual sense, beyond the letter. In Revelation 11:8, the great city where the two witnesses were killed is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt: the text does not literally refer to these ancient places, but uses them as images to describe the sin and spiritual oppression of that city.
G4153.origine: The word comes from πνεῦμα (pneuma, the Spirit, the breath) and carries the meaning of "in the manner of the Spirit." The root evokes the breath of life and divine power. It is the adverb formed from the adjective πνευματικός (pneumatikos, spiritual), which in the Greek Old Testament often translates Hebrew terms expressing the invisible and divine reality in contrast to mortal flesh.
G4153.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 2:14, it expresses the condition required to grasp God's revelations: one must be judged by the Spirit, having an understanding inhabited by the Spirit. In Revelation 11:8, it indicates that certain realities of the text must be interpreted in their spiritual, symbolic sense, rather than literally. Both usages emphasize the central role of the Holy Spirit in understanding the Word of God and in reading the spiritual signs of Revelation.
G4153.portee: This word reminds Christians that understanding divine things does not rely solely on human reason, but requires the presence and teaching of the Holy Spirit. It also invites the reader of Revelation to go beyond the literal sense and grasp the spiritual realities hidden beneath prophetic symbols. It is a call to cultivate spiritual sensitivity and not remain confined to a carnal and superficial reading.

sens: To breathe, to exhale air from the lungs
To move by running (referring to the wind)
To produce movement, agitation (referring to the wind on water or objects)
G4154.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to breathe or exhale: it is the natural action of vital breath. This elementary sense, inherent to living beings, underlies all other uses of the word.

2. The wind "blows": it is its own continuous movement. Jesus in John 3:8 uses this image to speak of the wind: "The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear the sound of it, but cannot tell where it comes from and where it goes." The wind is unpredictable, invisible in itself; one only perceives its effect.

3. When the wind blows strongly, it produces visible and powerful effects. In Matthew 7:25-27, the winds blow against a house and make it shake or collapse depending on its foundation. In John 6:18, a great wind was blowing that stirred up the sea. The verb then describes the action of the wind as a force that shakes, stirs, or carries away.
G4154.origine: The Greek word πνέω comes from a root that expresses the idea of air movement and breathing. In Hebrew, the verbs נָשַׁב (nashab) and נָשַׁף (nashaf) express breath and wind; the Greek translation of the Old Testament often renders them by πνέω. The word is related to πνεῦμα (pneuma, the spirit, the breath) and to πνοή (pnoé, the breath, the wind).
G4154.emploi: The verb πνέω appears 7 times in the New Testament, almost always in the concrete sense of the wind blowing. Matthew 7:25, 27 features it in the parable of the two houses: the winds blow against the constructions. Luke 12:55 uses it for weather observation: when the south wind blows, one knows it will be hot. John 3:8 makes it an image of the movement of the Holy Spirit, unpredictable and invisible. John 6:18 describes a violent wind stirring the lake. Acts 27:40 speaks of the wind used for sailing. Revelation 7:1 mentions the four winds of the earth. The word always designates the physical and natural phenomenon of wind.
G4154.portee: This word reminds the believer that the wind, like the Spirit of God, is an invisible power whose effects are the only visible signs. Jesus uses it to teach that the work of the Holy Spirit escapes our control and complete understanding. The wind that blows on the houses in Matthew 7 also symbolizes the trials that test the solidity of our spiritual foundation.

sens: Compress the throat to prevent breathing
Tighten someone's neck with force
Be overwhelmed by water and lose breath
G4155.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to compress or block the throat, preventing air from passing. In Matthew 13:7, the thorns "suffocate" the seeds by enclosing them and depriving them of the space and air necessary for their growth.
2. The verb also refers to the action of tightening someone's neck with the intent of violence or strangulation. In Matthew 18:28, the servant "strangles" his fellow servant by seizing him by the throat to force him to pay his debt.
3. By extension, to suffocate can mean to be overwhelmed or drowned in water: in Mark 5:13, the pigs rush into the sea and "drown," meaning they are suffocated by the water filling their lungs.
G4155.origine: The Greek verb πνίγω comes from a root expressing the idea of compression or constriction of the throat. It is related to Greek words that evoke asphyxiation and strangulation. The Hebrew word בָּעַת (bâ'at), used in 1 Kings 16:14-15, also means "suffocate" or "suppress" and describes a brutal action that deprives of breath or life.
G4155.emploi: The verb πνίγω appears three times in the New Testament with three distinct nuances. In Matthew 13:7, it describes the fate of the seeds suffocated by the thorns in the parable of the sower: it is a gradual process of suffocation. In Matthew 18:28, it expresses a voluntary and violent act of strangulation, the merciless servant physically seizing his fellow servant. In Mark 5:13, used in the passive voice, it means to be drowned: the herd of pigs is overwhelmed by the water and perishes asphyxiated. These three uses show that the verb always describes a deprivation of breath, through compression, strangulation, or submersion.
G4155.portee: This word reminds the reader of the forces that can suffocate the Word in our lives — the cares of the world (Matthew 13) — as well as the consequences of a lack of mercy towards others (Matthew 18). It shows how divine judgment can seem violent and inevitable for those who persist in unbelief (Mark 5). It is an invitation to cultivate an openness of heart to the Word and kindness towards others.

sens: Meat from an animal killed by strangulation or asphyxiation, without blood being shed
What is forbidden to believers of pagan origin in the first Christian assembly
G4156.detail:
1. The word refers to the flesh of an animal whose breath has been stopped, without shedding its blood: this was a practice forbidden to Jews by the Law of Moses (Leviticus 17:13-14), for the blood is life, and only God can take it back. Such meat was not ritually "slaughtered."

2. In Jerusalem, the apostles impose this abstinence on converted non-Jews, alongside three other rules (idolatry, blood, sexual immorality). It is a minimal rule of dietary purity, not for justification, but to allow Jewish and pagan believers to share meals (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25). The prohibition protects the respect due to life and the conscience of those coming from Judaism.
G4156.origine: The Greek word πνικτός (pniktos) comes from the verb πνίγω (pnigô), "to suffocate, to strangle." The image is that of breath stopped, death by asphyxiation. This word translates the Hebrew concept of meat not ritually slaughtered, an important subject in Jewish dietary laws.
G4156.emploi: The word appears only three times, solely in Acts, during the first council of Jerusalem (around A.D. 49). It is found in the apostolic decree addressed to the churches (Acts 15:20, 29), then recalled by James regarding converted pagans (Acts 21:25). The inclusion of this rule alongside blood shows that strangled meat and meat from which blood has not been shed were equated: both represented a violation of the respect for life according to the Law.
G4156.portee: This prohibition reminds us that, even freed by Christ from the entire Law, believers are not without limits: the conscience of others and respect for life remain important. It is a lesson on love and fellowship: "Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains" (Romans 14:3). For us, this invites reflection on food not as an individual whim, but as an act that can build up or harm the body of Christ.

sens: Movement of air, wind
Act of breathing, respiration
Vital principle that animates a living being
G4157.detail:
1. Breath is primarily the movement of air that one feels physically: it is a wind, a gust. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit arrives "like a mighty rushing wind that filled the entire house" (Acts 2:2) — not a true wind, but something that manifests as the wind would, sudden and powerful.
2. Breath also refers to the act of breathing, the vital breath exchanged between a living being and the air. God "gives to all life, breath, and all things" (Acts 17:25): it is He who allows creatures to live and breathe.
3. By extension, breath becomes the very principle of life, what keeps a being alive. This is why the Hebrew word it often translates (נְשָׁמָה, "neshamah") refers both to breath and the breath of life that God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7).
G4157.origine: The word comes from the verb πνέω ("pneô"), which means "to blow" or "to breathe." It describes the action of air in motion, either outside (the wind) or inside a living body (the breath). In Hebrew, נְשָׁמָה ("neshamah") has the same dual resonance: it is both the breath one breathes and the divine breath that gives life. Both words share this powerful image of breath as a sign and instrument of life.
G4157.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both times in Acts, with two nuances. In Acts 2:2, it is the mighty wind that accompanies the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost — a visible and audible manifestation of the divine. In Acts 17:25, it is the breath that God grants to all living beings, the foundation of their existence. These two uses show how the same word can describe both a natural force and a divine gift: the breath of the wind becomes an image of the breath of life that God gives.
G4157.portee: This word reminds us that life itself comes from God: it is He who makes us breathe at every moment. Every breath is a gift received from His hands. At Pentecost, the "mighty breath" from heaven speaks of the gift of the Holy Spirit, who renews and revitalizes the disciples. Meditating on breath is to become aware of our dependence on our Creator.

sens: Garment that extends to the feet
Tunic or robe worn by priests and important figures
Image of dignity and authority worn
G4158.detail:
1. A robe or tunic that extends to the feet, unlike ordinary clothing that stopped at the knees or calves. The Greek word combines the idea of foot (πούς) and length, literally forming "that goes down to the foot".
2. In the Old Testament, this type of long garment was worn by priests and high-ranking individuals: priests wore it to perform their service in the temple (see the translation of the Hebrew מְעִיל, the priestly garment). It was a sign of status and consecration.
3. In Revelation 1:13, the risen Christ appears dressed in a long robe, symbolizing his royal and priestly dignity: "someone like a son of man, dressed in a long robe, and with a golden sash around his chest." This image presents him in all his majesty.
G4158.origine: The Greek word comes from the root πούς (pous, "foot"). It literally designates a garment that extends "to the feet." In classical Greek, the term applies to long garments worn by dignitaries. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it primarily renders the Hebrew מְעִיל (meïl, the priest's garment) and other Hebrew terms designating priestly robes, showing that it was a costume of consecration and authority.
G4158.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: Revelation 1:13. In this passage, John describes the vision of the risen Lord in the midst of the seven lampstands, dressed in a long robe with a golden sash at the waist. This description recalls the Old Testament, where such garments distinguished priests and kings. The length of the garment down to the feet evokes the fullness of status, dignity, and authority. It is an intentional detail of the apocalyptic vision to present Christ in his glory.
G4158.portee: This image of Christ dressed in a long robe reminds Christians that the risen Lord reigns in absolute dignity and priestly authority. It invites contemplation not only of Christ's power but also of his role of intercession and perfect sacrifice. The priestly garment also evokes that every Christian is called to participate in this priesthood in their life of prayer and intercession.

sens: From which place, from what location (question about geographical origin)
How, by what means (question about cause or manner)
From what background, from what origin (question about social or familial provenance)
How can it be (expression of astonishment or incomprehension)
G4159.detail:
1. The basic meaning is spatial: "where do you come from?", "where does this come from?". In John 3:8, Jesus asks "where does the wind come from?" when speaking of the Spirit. It is simply the starting point of a journey or action.

2. The question shifts towards cause and means: "how" (by what process) something occurs. Mark 8:4: the disciples ask "how" to feed the crowd — it is no longer "where" in the geographical sense, but "by what means".

3. The question then concerns identity, status, or family origin. Matthew 13:56: "where" does he get all this? In John 7:27-28, people discuss "where" the Messiah comes from — his provenance in a broad sense.

4. It becomes an exclamation or objection: "how" can this be? Luke 1:43: Elizabeth exclaims "how is it granted to me" that Mary should come — it is astonishment at the improbable.
G4159.origine: This Greek word is an interrogative adverb formed from the prefix "po-" (as in "posos": how many) and the root "-then" (corresponding to the notion of place and origin). It primarily expresses a question of location or provenance. In translating the Greek Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew "ayin" (where?), which poses questions of both spatial and causal or identity nature.
G4159.emploi: The adverb "pothen" appears 26 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. It divides into three uses: (1) question of place — Luke 13:25: "where are you from?"; (2) question of cause or means — Mark 12:37: "how" can he be the son of David if David calls him Lord?; (3) question of origin or identity — Matthew 13:54: "where" does he get this wisdom? John 1:48: Nathanael is astonished: "where" do you know me from? The word thus shifts from the concrete (a place) to the complex (an explanation, a status).
G4159.portee: This small word reveals how the disciples and the crowds, faced with Jesus and his acts, ask fundamental questions: where does he come from? How does he operate? These inquiries are never neutral — they express confusion, disbelief, or admiration in the face of what exceeds ordinary explanation. For the Christian reader, these "where" questions indicate that believing in Jesus requires renouncing the obvious and recognizing a mysterious, divine origin.

sens: Create, produce, cause something
Accomplish an action, execute a task
Manufacture, prepare something concrete
Act, conduct oneself in a certain way
Practice, implement regularly
G4160G.detail:
1. Create or produce: the most direct meaning, particularly used for God who creates. Matthew 19:4: "Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female?"

2. Accomplish an action, execute a task: do what is asked of us, fulfill a will. Matthew 1:24: "When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him."

3. Manufacture or prepare a concrete object: build, prepare a meal, organize an event. Matthew 22:2: the king who "made a wedding feast for his son."

4. Act, conduct oneself in a certain way: the manner in which one behaves, whether good or bad. Matthew 12:12: "It is lawful to do good on the Sabbath."

5. Practice or implement regularly: express through action what one professes or believes. John 9:31: "We know that God does not listen to sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him."
G4160G.origine: The verb ποιέω (poieō) comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "to make" or "to create." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it generally translates the verb עשׂה (asah), which is the most common and broad action verb in Hebrew, meaning "to do" in a very general sense. This root exists in classical Greek with the same meaning: a ποιητής (poiètès) is a "poet," literally one who "makes" or "creates" words. The verb has retained this creative production force through the ages.
G4160G.emploi: The verb ποιέω is the action verb par excellence of the New Testament, used over 500 times. It appears in all books, particularly in Matthew, Luke, and John. Its varied meaning depends on the context: with a direct object designating a creation (Acts 19:11: God "was doing" miracles), it means "to create" or "to produce"; with an abstract verb or noun (John 9:31: "to do his will"), it means "to accomplish" or "to realize"; with an adverb (Mark 7:37: "He has done all things well"), it expresses the manner of the action. The key distinction is between a punctuated action (ποιέω) and an established habit (πράσσω): ποιέω shows the particular act, while πράσσω suggests a regular practice.
G4160G.portee: Understanding this verb allows one to grasp the moral responsibility that runs through the entire Gospel: faith is not reduced to words; it is demonstrated through actions. Doing the will of God, doing good, doing the truth: these expressions recur to remind the reader that the profession of Christian faith must be embodied in concrete actions. It is a call to practical obedience and transformation of behavior.

sens: To produce, create, manufacture something new
To accomplish, execute an action, realize what one intends
To prepare, organize an event or a meal
To observe, practice, implement a law or commandment
To spend time
G4160H.detail:
1. To produce or create: this is the most concrete meaning, that of manufacturing or bringing something into existence. God "made" man in His image (Matthew 19:4); a craftsman makes clothing (Acts 9:39); or forming the earth as a potter shapes his clay (Romans 9:20).

2. To accomplish, execute: to do an action means to carry it out, to execute it. This can be simple (to make a gesture) or serious (to make a promise), and the word adapts to all kinds of acts: "What are you doing?" one asks someone who is accomplishing something.

3. To prepare, organize: to make a meal or a feast means to prepare it, to set it up. John recounts that Jesus eats with Levi, who "made a great feast" (Luke 5:29) in His honor.

4. To practice, observe: to do the law or commandments means to put them into practice, to truly observe them. Jesus says that one must "do" justice, not just know it.

5. To spend: to do or pass time means to consume it, to spend it (Matthew 20:12 or Revelation 13:5).
G4160H.origine: The Greek verb ποιέω comes from an ancient root that literally means "to do, to make" and evokes creative or productive action. In Hebrew, it primarily translates עשׂה (asah), the most common verb for "to do" or "to create." It is a very rich verb: it encompasses all human or divine action, from the simplest gesture to the creative work. The word family includes ποιητής (poet, one who creates), ποίησις (creation, composition), and many other derivatives.
G4160H.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament, used in all the books and in very varied contexts. It primarily expresses the divine action of creation (God makes the world, living beings). It then describes human acts: making a promise, making a meal, making a road. It is also used for moral or religious actions: doing justice, doing the law, doing good works. Notably, there is an important nuance: the New Testament distinguishes it from πράσσω (prattō), which emphasizes habit or repeated practice, while ποιέω can describe a unique action or the act in general. In Romans 9:20, the potter who "made" the vessel illustrates divine creative action: it is God who shapes as the potter shapes the clay.
G4160H.portee: This verb reminds us that our life, our choices, our acts materialize what we believe and what we love. When the Bible asks the believer to "do" justice or to "do" the commandments, it is not speaking of simple theoretical knowledge, but of concrete implementation. It is an invitation not to settle for words or good intentions, but to truly act. The contrast between God who "does" all things and man who contests it (Romans 9:20) humbles us: our acts are small before the One who created the universe.

sens: To produce, create, manufacture something material or immaterial
To accomplish an action, execute a task, realize something
To obtain a result, produce an effect through an action
To establish, institute, set up an organization or a person
To constitute, form, render (with an attribute)
To habitually practice, conduct oneself in a certain manner
G4160I.detail:
1. To produce or create: to manufacture something, to bring it into existence. God "made" man and woman (general reference to the source); a craftsman "makes" a purse (Luke 12:33) or clothing (Acts 9:39 cited in the source).

2. To accomplish, execute: to realize an action, to carry out what one must do. Paul "does" not regard his life (Acts 20:24), meaning he does not consider it important; it is the action of holding something as nothing.

3. To produce an effect: to generate a result through one's action. Peter's speech "makes" him recognized (Matthew 26:73), meaning it reveals his identity by the effect it produces.

4. To establish, institute: to create or found a lasting structure, notably a charge or a group. Jesus "established" twelve apostles (Mark 3:14), meaning He designates and constitutes them in this role.

5. To constitute, render: to transform something by endowing it with a new quality or nature. When it says "here are the twelve" (Mark 3:16), this verb inscribes this formation of a group into reality.

6. To practice, have the habit: to act according to a certain way of living, regularly or characteristically. To be or not to be in a moral or practical habit.
