G4160I.origine: From the classical Greek poieō, this verb originally means "to shape, to manufacture" (an Indo-European root common to the words "poet," "poetry"). In biblical Greek, it primarily translates the Hebrew עשׂה (asah), which covers a very broad field: to do, to make, to act, to accomplish. It is an extremely common verb, capable of expressing almost any human or divine action. It also establishes the concept of "poiesis" (creation) and is never limited to a simple doing: it includes intention, result, duration.
G4160I.emploi: Poieō is the most frequent general action verb in the New Testament. It indiscriminately designates material action (to manufacture an object, Acts 9:39), moral action (to accomplish justice, Matthew 6:1 cited in the source), or institutional action (to establish the apostles, Mark 3:14). Its meaning is specified by the complement: with an object noun, it describes creation or confection; with a nominalized action verb (a race, a service), it creates a periphrasis to express the complete act. Mark 3:14–16 clearly shows this versatility: "to establish" the twelve apostles, "here are" the names (the act of presentation). In Paul (Acts 20:24), it marks the voluntary commitment to a mission. The distinction with the verb prasso (to do, to act) is that poieō emphasizes the result, the outcome, while prasso stresses habitual or repeated action.
G4160I.portee: This verb reminds us that the Christian must not only "believe" or "say," but "do" — transforming faith into concrete acts, intentions into visible results. Jesus establishes the apostles not in theory, but by choosing and constituting them for the mission (Mark 3:14). For Paul, "doing" his race means concretely fulfilling what has been entrusted, without being deterred by the fear of death (Acts 20:24). The verb invites the reader to measure their faith by their works, to ask: what am I really "doing" with my vocation, my possessions, my life?

sens: Accomplir une période, une durée en un lieu ou une activité
Parcourir un trajet ou traverser une région
Laisser s'écouler une durée déterminée
Consacrer du temps à une action
S'engager à rester quelque part pendant une période
G4160J.detail: 1. Accomplir une période déterminée en un lieu donné : le mot signifie achever ou mener à terme un laps de temps spécifié. En Acts 18:23, Paul « passa quelque temps à Antioche » avant de repartir en mission, marquant ainsi une étape complète de son voyage. 2. Parcourir un trajet ou traverser une région en se déplaçant : c'est l'idée de progresser d'un endroit à un autre au cours du temps. Acts 20:3 l'illustre : après avoir séjourné trois mois en Grèce, Paul décida de « reprendre la route de la Macédoine », passant ainsi par différents territoires. 3. Laisser s'écouler une durée sans intervention particulière : c'est simplement consommer du temps. En Acts 15:33, après un délai (« au bout de quelque temps »), les frères reçoivent congé. 4. Consacrer intentionnellement du temps à une action ou un objectif : dans James 4:13, le riche projette de « passer une année » en ville pour y faire du commerce, investissant délibérément cette durée. 5. S'engager à demeurer quelque part pour une période fixe : sous-entendu dans les projets humains où l'on détermine d'avance combien de temps on restera. En 2 Corinthians 11:25, Paul évoque avoir « passé un jour et une nuit dans l'abîme », durée subie mais clairement délimitée.
G4160J.origine: Le verbe grec ποιέω vient d'une racine désignant l'action de faire, produire ou créer. En hébreu biblique, il traduit très souvent le verbe עשׂה (asa, faire), qui exprime l'action générale sous tous ses aspects. Lorsque ποιέω est appliqué au temps, il reprend l'idée de fabriquer, créer ou constituer une durée : on « fait » le temps s'écouler comme on fabrique un objet. Cette extension du sens montre comment le grec biblique emprunte à la langue courante des images usuelles pour parler de réalités abstraites comme la durée.
G4160J.emploi: Le verbe ποιέω est extrêmement fréquent en grec du Nouveau Testament (plusieurs centaines d'occurrences). Lorsqu'il s'applique au temps, il apparaît surtout dans les récits de voyage et les projets humains : Acts 15:33, 18:23, 20:3 le montrent dans le contexte des voyages missionnaires de Paul ; James 4:13 dans un discours de sagesse critiquant les plans ambitieux des riches ; 2 Corinthians 11:25 énumère les épreuves endurées par Paul au cours de ses missions. Le sens varie légèrement selon le contexte : il peut marquer simplement le passage du temps (Acts 15:33), l'accomplissement d'une mission pendant une durée (Acts 18:23), ou l'intention de consacrer une période à une activité (James 4:13). Dans tous les cas, il souligne que le temps est délimité, mesuré et structurant.
G4160J.portee: Ce mot rappelle que le temps est un bien à gérer consciemment. Chez Paul, « passer du temps » dans l'accomplissement du ministère apostolique montre que le temps sert le service de Dieu et l'établissement des églises. Chez James, au contraire, vouloir « passer une année » en ville pour s'enrichir illustre l'illusion humaine de contrôler l'avenir, rappelant l'incertitude de la vie et l'appel à se soumettre à la volonté de Dieu. C'est une invitation à examiner comment nous dépensons nos jours : au service du Seigneur ou de nos propres projets.

sens: Ce qui a été fait ou créé par quelqu'un
Œuvre qui manifeste le talent ou la puissance de son auteur
Résultat d'un travail ou d'une création intentionnelle
G4161.detail:
1. Le mot désigne tout ce qui est fait, créé ou produit : c'est le résultat concret d'une action. En Romans 1:20, les ouvrages visibles de Dieu — le ciel, la terre, tout ce qu'on voit — témoignent de sa puissance éternelle.
2. C'est une œuvre qui révèle la main de celui qui l'a faite : un ouvrage bien fait montre le talent de l'artisan. En Ephesians 2:10, nous sommes nous-mêmes cet ouvrage de Dieu, créés pour montrer sa sagesse et son amour.
3. Le mot insiste sur l'intention et la planification : Dieu a préparé d'avance les bonnes œuvres (littéralement « les œuvres bonnes ») que nous devons accomplir, comme un artisan qui prépare son projet avant de le réaliser.
G4161.origine: Le mot vient du verbe « faire » (poiein en grec). Il désigne le produit fini d'une activité créatrice. La même racine produit le mot « poésie » : une poésie est aussi un ouvrage créé avec art. En hébreu, ce mot traduit souvent « maaséh », qui signifie « œuvre, travail, action » — le même mot que Dieu emploie quand il contemple son ouvrage à la création et voit que c'est bon.
G4161.emploi: Le mot n'apparaît que deux fois dans le Nouveau Testament. En Romans 1:20, Paul l'emploie pour désigner les créations visibles de Dieu (les créatures, le monde) qui révèlent son éternité et sa puissance. En Ephesians 2:10, il s'applique à nous-mêmes : nous sommes l'ouvrage de Dieu, le produit de sa création en Jésus-Christ. Dans ce second passage, Paul ajoute que cet ouvrage a une finalité — nous avons été créés pour accomplir les bonnes œuvres que Dieu a préparées. Le mot insiste toujours sur l'intention de créateur et sur la perfection du résultat.
G4161.portee: Pour le chrétien, ce mot rappelle deux vérités vivantes : d'abord, que l'univers visible — le ciel, la création — proclame la puissance et l'intelligence de Dieu et invite à le reconnaître et l'adorer ; ensuite, que chaque croyant est une œuvre personnelle de Dieu, créée non par hasard mais avec un projet précis, une destinée de bien et de service. Nous ne sommes pas des accidents : nous sommes des créations intentionnelles.

sens: celui qui crée ou compose une œuvre
poète, celui qui compose des vers
celui qui met en pratique, qui agit selon quelque chose
G4163.detail:
1. Au sens premier, c'est celui qui fait, qui crée ou fabrique quelque chose — l'auteur d'une œuvre. Le mot vient du verbe « faire » et garde cette idée de créativité et d'action productive.
2. Plus particulièrement, c'est un poète, quelqu'un qui compose des vers ou des œuvres littéraires (Acts 17:28, où Paul cite des « poètes » grecs).
3. De façon plus large et morale, c'est celui qui met en pratique, qui agit réellement : non pas celui qui écoute seulement la loi, mais celui qui la « met en pratique » (Romans 2:13), celui qui « se met à l'œuvre » (James 1:25), celui qui est « observateur » de la loi par ses actes (James 4:11). C'est le contraste avec le simple auditeur : la vraie foi se mesure à ce qu'on fait, pas à ce qu'on entend.
G4163.origine: Le mot vient du verbe grec « poiéô » qui signifie « faire, créer ». C'est pourquoi le poète était originellement celui qui « fait » la poésie — et par extension, celui qui accomplit, qui réalise, qui met en œuvre. La racine suggère toujours cette idée de passage de l'intention à l'action, de la parole au fait.
G4163.emploi: Le mot apparaît 6 fois dans le Nouveau Testament. Une seule fois au sens premier : « poète » (Acts 17:28, où Paul cite les poètes païens). Partout ailleurs, il désigne celui qui met en pratique, qui agit vraiment : la loi (Romans 2:13, James 4:11), la parole (James 1:22-23), l'œuvre (James 1:25). L'enjeu biblique est clair : dans ces passages de James et de Paul, le mot contraste toujours avec le simple auditeur ou le regardeur passif — c'est celui qui transforme la parole en action qui obtient la bénédiction.
G4163.portee: Ce mot parle au cœur : la foi chrétienne n'est pas une doctrine qu'on écoute et qu'on oublie, mais une vie qu'on vit. Être un véritable auditeur de la loi de Dieu, c'est en être un « auteur » ou un « metteur en pratique ». La vraie obéissance n'est jamais que théorique — elle change nos actes, nos paroles, notre quotidien.

sens: Of various kinds, different colors or aspects
That takes on multiple forms, several characters
That varies, which is not uniform
Multiplied, abundant in its variety
G4164.detail:
1. The primary, literal meaning is that of visible variety, particularly in colors or patterns: it is a variegated tapestry, fabrics adorned with various designs. This sense of nuance and diversity then applies to diseases (Matthew 4:24: "diseases of various kinds"), miracles (Hebrews 2:4: "various miracles"), and any reality that presents several different aspects.
2. The word is used figuratively to describe a variety of moral or spiritual forms: "various diseases" can mean both the different nature of infirmities and the multiplicity of afflictions of the body and soul. In 2 Timothy 3:6, "passions of all kinds" refers to the many desires that torment the weak soul.
3. In the context of Christian sufferings, the word emphasizes multiplicity and the absence of uniformity: James 1:2 speaks of "various trials" to show that faith is tested in many different ways, not just once in a single manner.
4. The term can finally express the idea of profusion, varied abundance: Titus 3:3 mentions "all kinds of desires," meaning the multitude of carnal desires that characterized the past life of the sinner.
G4164.origine: The Greek word poikilos comes from a root that evokes the idea of speckling, mixing, creating varied and colorful patterns. Its etymology refers to the image of the work of a embroiderer or painter who composes a work with mixed colors and diverse designs. The fundamental notion is that of variation in color or form, from which it extends to anything that takes on multiple aspects, characters, or forms. In Hebrew, the word sometimes corresponds to naqod ("spotted") or riqmah ("embroidery"), which confirms the initial image of visible and colorful diversity.
G4164.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, distributed across the Gospels, the pastoral epistles, and the general epistles. In the first three Gospels, it describes the various diseases from which Jesus healed the sick (Matthew 4:24, Mark 1:34, Luke 4:40), highlighting the multiplicity and variety of infirmities to which Jesus' power addresses. In Hebrews 2:4, it qualifies the various miracles by which God supports the testimony of the apostles. In moral and spiritual contexts, in 2 Timothy 3:6 and Titus 3:3, the word designates the multiplicity of carnal passions and desires that characterize sin. In the epistles of James and Peter, it evokes the variety of trials that faith encounters, emphasizing the diversity of temptations and sufferings that the believer endures. The meaning remains constant: to express variety, multiplicity, and the absence of uniformity.
G4164.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God, in His wisdom and power, masters the infinite variety of human evils — diseases, temptations, sufferings — and that He is capable of responding to each particular form of distress. Understanding that trials are "various" also helps the disciple not to believe that only one kind of suffering exists in the world, but to recognize the complexity of the sinful human condition and the inexhaustible richness of divine grace that responds to it.

sens: To graze a flock, to keep and feed it
To lead and care for a community or people as a shepherd tends to his sheep
G4165.detail:
1. To shepherd is primarily to be a shepherd: to lead the sheep to pasture, to keep them, to feed them. This is the daily work of the pastor. In Luke 17:7, we see a servant returning from the fields where he "shepherds" the flocks, as a normal and laborious task. In 1 Corinthians 9:7, the one who "shepherds" a flock has the right to eat its milk — an image of the work that nourishes the one who performs it.
2. To shepherd becomes a powerful image of governance and pastoral care. When Jesus says to Peter, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:16), He entrusts him with the responsibility of His Church — to guide, protect, and spiritually nourish it. In Acts 20:28, Paul exhorts the elders to "shepherd the Church of the Lord," meaning to govern it with the devotion and tenderness of a good shepherd. In 1 Peter 5:2, pastors must "shepherd" the flock of God willingly, not under compulsion or for gain. Even in Matthew 2:6, the Messiah to be born will "shepherd" Israel, His people — He will govern them with wisdom and kindness.
G4165.origine: The Greek word poimainô comes from poimên (shepherd). This verb translates the Hebrew raaah, which fundamentally means to lead to pasture. The metaphor of the shepherd and the flock is ancient and common in the ancient Near East: it expresses the idea that one who leads must take care of his people with vigilance, tenderness, and responsibility, like a shepherd for his sheep.
G4165.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. Literally, it describes the work of the shepherd (Luke 17:7, 1 Corinthians 9:7). But its major meaning is metaphorical and pastoral: Jesus entrusts Peter with the mission to "shepherd" His sheep (John 21:16), the apostles and elders are established to "shepherd" the Church (Acts 20:28, 1 Peter 5:2), and the Messiah will "shepherd" Israel (Matthew 2:6, echoing Psalm 23 and Micah 5:1). The word thus expresses the idea of governance, spiritual direction, and care for the people of God. The uses in Revelation (2:27, 7:17, 12:5, 19:15) apply this image to Christ who reigns.
G4165.portee: This verb shows that leading the Church or serving the people of God does not mean dominating or exploiting, but "shepherding" — that is, taking care, nourishing, protecting. For a pastor or Christian leader, it is a call to tenderness and dedication, not authoritarianism. And for every believer, it is a reminder that Christ "shepherds" His Church: we are His sheep, and He takes care of us with all the vigilance of a good shepherd.

sens: Man who guards and leads flocks of sheep
One who watches over a group of people by guiding and protecting them
Christ, who cares for His people like a shepherd for his sheep
Pastor or spiritual leader of a Christian community
G4166.detail:
1. A shepherd is literally one who keeps the sheep and leads them to pasture. The shepherds of Bethlehem who watched over their flocks at night (Luke 2:8) embody this humble and concrete profession: watching over the animals, protecting them from danger, and feeding them.

2. The image of the shepherd also describes one who cares for an entire people, guiding and protecting them. Jesus sees the crowd as "harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd" (Matthew 9:36): without guidance, people are lost and without help.

3. Christ Himself reveals Himself as "the good shepherd" who "lays down His life for the sheep" (John 10:11). He is not a shepherd who would abandon His flock in danger, but one who sacrifices Himself for it.

4. In Christian churches, pastors are called "shepherds" (Ephesians 4:11), as they are charged with watching over believers, spiritually feeding them, and keeping them in faith, just like a shepherd for his sheep.
G4166.origine: The Greek word "poimēn" comes from a root meaning "to feed" and "to keep." It regularly translates the Hebrew word "rāʿâh" (Psalm 23: "The Lord is my shepherd"), which designates one who leads and feeds a flock. This image is very ancient in the Near East: kings themselves were often compared to shepherds of their people.
G4166.emploi: The word "shepherd" appears 17 times in the New Testament, primarily in Matthew, Luke, and John. It first refers to historical shepherds: those of Bethlehem who watched over their flocks when the angels announced the birth of Jesus (Luke 2:8, 15, 20). Jesus then uses it in a prophecy about His passion: "I will strike the shepherd" (Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27), announcing His death and the scattering of the disciples. But most importantly, John 10 extensively develops the image of Christ as "the good shepherd" who knows His sheep, calls them by name, and lays down His life for them (John 10:11, 14). Finally, the term describes the spiritual leaders of the Church, the pastors that God gives to communities to nourish and guide them (Ephesians 4:11).
G4166.portee: This image reveals who Jesus is and how He loves us: not by dominating from afar, but by personally watching over each of His disciples, knowing them by name, and dying for them. It also shows that Christian leaders are not commanding chiefs, but serving shepherds, called to nourish, protect, and guide God's flock with tenderness and dedication.

sens: Group of sheep or goats kept together
Set of sheep entrusted to a shepherd
Image of the Church, the people of believers under the guidance of Christ
G4167.detail:
1. The flock is primarily a group of animals, mainly sheep, living and moving together under the care of a shepherd. It is a concrete fact of pastoral life: in Bethlehem, the shepherds kept their flocks at night in the fields (Luke 2:8), and the flocks could be large (Matthew 26:31).
2. The shepherd who pastures a flock derives his sustenance from it — milk, wool, sometimes meat — which shows the interdependence of the pastor and his flock (1 Corinthians 9:7: "Who serves as a shepherd and does not eat of the flock's milk?").
3. Jesus uses this image to speak of His disciples: "I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also; they will hear My voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd" (John 10:16). The flock becomes the image of the Church gathered around Christ, the good shepherd.
G4167.origine: The word comes from the family of "shepherd" (poimen in Greek) and designates what belongs to the shepherd. The image of the flock is fundamental in the Old Testament Bible: the patriarchs, Moses, and David were shepherds, and God Himself is often presented as the shepherd of Israel. The New Testament takes up this image to describe the relationship of Christ with the Church.
G4167.emploi: The word ποίμνη appears four times in the New Testament, always applied to sheep or metaphorically to the Church. In the Gospels, it refers to the actual flocks kept by the shepherds of Bethlehem (Luke 2:8) or cited in reference to Psalm 23 about the shepherd who abandons his sheep (Matthew 26:31). In Paul, it is a concrete example of the shepherd who lives from his work (1 Corinthians 9:7). In John, the image becomes entirely spiritual: Christ's unique flock gathers believers from all backgrounds who listen to His voice. The progression goes from the literal sense to the figurative sense of the mystery of the Church.
G4167.portee: This word reminds the believer that he is part of a community, the flock of Christ, and that he hears the voice of his shepherd. It is a reassuring and humble image: it conveys both the protection of the attentive pastor and the smallness of each sheep. It also invites reflection on the unity of the Church despite the diversity of its members.

sens: Group of sheep or other livestock kept together
Set of faithful in a Christian community, entrusted to a pastor
G4168.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a real flock, a group of sheep grazing together under the care of a shepherd (this is the primary image). 2. In speaking of Christians, Jesus and the apostles use this image to show how the faithful form a united community, entrusted to the leaders of the Church. Jesus calls the disciples a "little flock" to which the Father wants to give the kingdom (Luke 12:32); Paul exhorts the elders to "shepherd the flock of God" (Acts 20:28), and not to dominate over it but to be examples (1 Peter 5:2-3). The image of the flock emphasizes both the unity of the body of Christ and the responsibility of pastors for those entrusted to them.
G4168.origine: The Greek word ποίμνιον comes from the root ποιμ- (to pasture, to keep). It is a variant of ποίμνη, a word of the same meaning but less common in the New Testament. In Hebrew, words like צֹאן (flock of sheep) or עֵדֶר (flock in general) are used to express the idea of gathered livestock. The image of the shepherd and the flock was familiar to the people of Israel and runs throughout the Bible.
G4168.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in an ecclesial context, never for a real flock of animals. Jesus uses it once (Luke 12:32) to reassure His disciples. Paul and Peter use it several times to speak of the responsibility of pastors: in Acts 20, Paul warns the elders of Ephesus that false pastors, "savage wolves," will threaten the flock. In 1 Peter 5, Peter emphasizes the duty of the elders to "shepherd" the flock, that is, to spiritually nourish and protect it, without exercising arrogant domination. The word always evokes unity, vulnerability, and the need for spiritual care.
G4168.portee: This image of the flock invites the Christian to recognize himself as a member of a united community, under the care of a divine Shepherd. For the leaders of the Church, it reminds them that they are called not to dominate but to serve, to nourish, and protect those entrusted to them. For all believers, it expresses both security (belonging to a cared-for flock) and mutual responsibility (being interdependent like the sheep of the same flock).

sens: Direct interrogative: what kind, what nature?
Indirect interrogative: what kind, what nature (in a reported question)
Interrogative about the identity or qualities of a person
G4169.detail:
1. The word expresses a question about the quality, nature, or type of something. It is the interrogative "what?" used in the face of several possibilities. For example: "What is the first of all the commandments?" (Mark 12:28), where one asks which commandment is the most important.
2. In indirect questions, this word reports an inquiry without posing it directly: "he indicated what kind of death he was to die" (John 18:32), meaning it reports what type of death was concerned.
3. The word can also inquire about the identity or specific characteristics of a person: "What is this man?" or "What circumstances?" The meaning always remains that of seeking to know the quality, nature, or type.
G4169.origine: PoÏos comes from ancient Greek and corresponds to the demonstrative "such" and the relative interrogative "who, what." It is a basic interrogative word formed to ask "of what kind?" or "what type?" In ancient translations of the Old Testament into Greek, it often translates the Hebrew "eï-zeh" (literally "what?") and related forms. The word belongs to the family of qualification and distinction.
G4169.emploi: PoÏos appears 32 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and in the epistles. It is mainly used to formulate direct questions about the nature or type of something: "What day?" (Matthew 24:42), "What death?" (John 18:32), "What commandment?" (Mark 12:28). It is also found in indirect questions, where it reports an inquiry: "she was seeking by what circumstance" (Luke 5:19). In all cases, it is a tool for questioning the quality, category, or identity of a reality. The context determines whether the question pertains to a person, an act, a moment, or a principle.
G4169.portee: This word invites the reader to examine the true nature of things. When the Bible asks "What day?" or "What commandment?", it pushes us not to live in indifference, but to seek to know the important things: the will of God, the right moment, the order of spiritual priorities. It is a word of discernment and vigilance.

sens: To engage in war, an armed combat
To struggle against an opponent, in a figurative sense
To oppose, resist someone or something
G4170.detail:
1. To fight primarily means to make war, to confront an enemy with weapons in hand — this is the literal sense of the word. In Revelation 12:7, Michael and his angels "fight" against the dragon: it is a real but spiritual heavenly battle.
2. The word is also used in a figurative sense for opposition, a struggle that is less physical but just as real. In Revelation 2:16, Jesus says: "I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth" — here, to fight means to oppose those who refuse to repent, by His powerful word.
3. The word can refer to a quarrel, a dispute between people. In James 4:2, Paul speaks of those who "have quarrels and fights" — to fight here means to dispute, to confront through hostile words or actions, without necessarily involving war in the literal sense.
G4170.origine: The verb to fight comes from the Greek word πόλεμος (polemos), meaning war. It is an active word, denoting action: it does not describe the state of conflict, but the act of fighting. In Hebrew, in the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the verb "לָחַם" (lahham), which literally means "to eat bread together" but has come to mean "to make war" — probably because two armies would meet and confront each other.
G4170.emploi: The verb to fight appears six times in the provided usages, almost exclusively in Revelation (5 times) and once in the epistle of James. In Revelation, it first describes the great heavenly war between Michael and the dragon (12:7), then the eschatological battles: the beast that fights against the faithful (17:14), the Lamb who will conquer (17:14, 19:11). Jesus also "fights" against those who refuse His call to repentance (2:16). In James 4:2, the usage is closer to everyday life: it concerns quarrels and disputes among Christians, due to their desires. The word thus oscillates between true warrior combat and figurative, spiritual, or interpersonal struggle.
G4170.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian life is a struggle, a conflictual reality: spiritual conflict against evil and against our own passions (James 4:2), but also assured victory if we remain faithful to the Lamb (Revelation 17:14). It teaches us that Jesus' fight is not a defeat or passivity, but a powerful and justified action against evil. This verb calls us to rise from apathy and recognize that our faith is not neutral in the face of evil.

sens: Armed conflict between nations or peoples
Combat, confrontation between fighters
Noise and clamor of battle
Quarrel, struggle between people
G4171.detail:
1. War is the armed conflict between nations or groups: "You will hear of wars" (Matthew 24:6) announces the great conflicts that will mark future times. It implies organization, preparations, like a king who counts his forces before confronting an enemy (Luke 14:31).
2. Combat refers to the direct confrontation between fighters or armies: the trumpet of battle calls soldiers to prepare for the noise of battle (1 Corinthians 14:8). It is the action of war itself, the clash of arms.
3. The noise and tumult characterize the battle: the sound of the locusts' wings resembles the noise of chariots rushing into battle (Revelation 9:9), an image of terrifying magnitude.
4. By extension, struggle and quarrel between people: James thus refers to the internal conflicts of Christians, born from their opposing desires (James 4:1). The "war" can be spiritual: Michael and his angels fight the dragon in heaven (Revelation 12:7).
G4171.origine: The Greek word polemos literally means "conflict" or "hostility." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word milkhama (מִלְחָמָה) to denote war. The Greek root evokes the idea of opposition and confrontation. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), polemos regularly translates milkhama. The word belongs to the family of the verb polemeo (to make war).
G4171.emploi: The word polemos appears 16 times in the New Testament, especially in Revelation (8 occurrences) and in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. In the Synoptic Gospels, it refers to the eschatological wars announced before the end times (Matthew 24:6, Mark 13:7, Luke 21:9). Paul uses it for the warrior's combat who must know the signal of the trumpet (1 Corinthians 14:8). James uses it metaphorically for human quarrels (James 4:1). Revelation makes it a central theme: heavenly wars (12:7), battles of the dragon and his enemies (12:17, 13:7, 16:14, 19:19, 20:8). Hebrews 11:34 mentions the wars won by the heroes of faith. The word can refer to both massive military operations and small quarrels, from the greatest conflict to the most intimate.
G4171.portee: Understanding the word "war" in the New Testament helps the Christian grasp the seriousness of the conflicts to come and the reality of spiritual struggle. Jesus warns that wars and rumors of wars should not disturb faith (Matthew 24:6): the believer must remain confident despite the upheavals of the world. James applies the image to quarrels among Christians, urging them to recognize that they stem from guilty passions: it is an invitation to peace. Revelation reveals that the ultimate conflict will be won by Christ.

sens: urban agglomeration with its buildings, inhabitants, and structures
the collective of the inhabitants of a city
region or territory controlled by a city
place of residence of a person
in apocalyptic language, heavenly dwelling or eschatological gathering place
Jerusalem, the holy city
G4172.detail:
1. A city is primarily an agglomeration: a populated space gathering houses, streets, and public places. Mark 1:33 shows the entire crowd of a city gathered at the door of Simon Peter, illustrating how a city is a center of dense population. Luke 4:29 speaks of the city of Nazareth where Jesus grew up, a specific and identifiable geographical location.
2. Often the word refers to the inhabitants themselves: the city that reacts, the city that sees, the city that speaks. In Matthew 21:10, "the whole city was stirred," it is not the walls that are stirred, but the people who live there. This is a natural synecdoche: we say "the city" to mean "the citizens."
3. A city also commands a region around it: its territory, its fields, its villages. Acts 16:14 mentions Lydia "from the city of Thyatira," designating not only the agglomeration but the entire area it controls.
4. The word can also refer to the place where someone lives or is from, their homeland. Luke 2:4 speaks of the city of David, that of Judea from which Joseph's family came, emphasizing attachment and roots.
5. In Revelation, it takes on a spiritual dimension: it refers to the heavenly City, the new Jerusalem that believers await, an eschatological dwelling. Hebrews 13:14 expresses this: "for we seek the one to come."
6. Jerusalem receives special titles: "holy city" (Matthew 4:5) or "beloved city" (Revelation 20:9), reflecting its unique role in the history of salvation.
G4172.origine: The word πόλις comes from an ancient Greek root and designates the political and social center of collective life. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament regularly translates עִיר ("ir") as πόλις: these two words cover the same reality — a fortified inhabited place, a center of administration and exchange. The Greek word has enriched itself in Hellenistic culture, where the polis referred to both the physical agglomeration and the civic and political community it housed. The family of the word produces few common derivatives in New Testament Greek, but it is central to the ancient conception of organized life.
G4172.emploi: The word πόλις (city) appears more than 150 times in the New Testament, notably in Luke, who loves to narrate the expansion of the Christian message from city to city. It primarily designates specific named cities: Nazareth (Matthew 2:23), Bethlehem (Luke 2:4), Ephraim (John 11:54). Often it is contrasted with villages (κῶμαι) and fields: Matthew 9:35 shows Jesus teaching "in their synagogues and preaching the gospel of the kingdom in every city and every village." The Apostle Paul travels from city to city, proclaiming the Gospel to Jews and Gentiles (Acts 16:14; 21:30 mentions urban conflicts). A figurative usage clearly distinguishes the "permanent city" (Hebrews 13:14) — unstable, earthly — from the one that "is to come," heavenly. Jerusalem holds a special place: it is the "holy city" par excellence, sanctified by the temple and the presence of God.
G4172.portee: For the Christian reader, this notion of city invites recognition of where human life truly unfolds: in places of common habitation, decision-making, and encounters. It is in cities that Jesus and the apostles proclaim the Gospel — an affirmation that salvation is offered at the heart of organized life, not in escape. But above all, the contrast between the earthly city (unstable, "permanent") and the heavenly City teaches that the Christian is but a pilgrim here below: their true rest, their true homeland, is with God. This reminder of our heavenly citizenship purifies our relationship with earthly places and institutions.

sens: Administrative and judicial official of a city
Official responsible for maintaining public order
G4173.detail:
1. The magistrate is an administrative official placed at the head of a city to govern and render justice. In Acts 17:6, when the crowd of Thessalonica drags Jason before the magistrates, they address the official authorities capable of settling disputes and punishing wrongdoers.
2. The magistrate is also one who represents public order and can be moved, agitated by serious accusations (Acts 17:8). He embodies the civil power established by the government, distinct from ordinary people.
G4173.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: πόλις (polis), meaning "city," and the verb meaning "to reign" or "to command." It literally designates one who reigns over the city. It is a specifically Greek word that Roman historians of the time noted as an official title in the Greek cities of Macedonia, particularly in Thessalonica.
G4173.emploi: The word appears only twice in Acts 17, regarding the magistrates of Thessalonica. When jealous Jews of Paul's success incite a riot, they drag Jason (a believer) and others before these civil authorities (verses 6 and 8). The magistrates are supposed to maintain peace and judge accusations: here, they are accused of harboring troublemakers. The word always designates municipal officers recognized by the Roman government in Greek cities.
G4173.portee: This passage shows how the Gospel provokes a reaction from civil power and how established authorities are confronted with the message of Christ. For the reader, this reminds us that faith does not spread in a vacuum: it confronts institutions and officials, who must respond. It is also a historical indication of Luke's precision, who uses the exact term for the administrative office in Thessalonica.

sens: Legal status of a citizen, with the rights and duties attached to belonging to a city or state
Power to govern a community, administration
Political community, commonwealth, the collective of citizens forming a state
G4174.detail: 1. It is the legal status that makes one belong to a city and enjoy its rights: being a Roman citizen means having this "citizenship," a precious status that can only be acquired by inheritance or exception (Acts 22:28). 2. By extension, it is also the power to govern this community, the administration and political order itself. 3. Finally, it is the political entity formed by the citizens — the city itself as a community united by laws. When Paul tells the Ephesians that they were "without citizenship in Israel" (Ephesians 2:12), he means that as Gentiles, they did not belong to the people of Israel, to the covenants and promises of God; they were strangers to this holy community.
G4174.origine: The word comes from the Greek πολίτης (politès), meaning "citizen," which itself derives from πόλις (polis), meaning "city." The latter word evokes communal life in an ancient city-state, organized by laws. The "politeia" is therefore primarily the way this city lives together, its regime. The word has designated in classical Greek not only citizenship but also the Constitution, the form of government — we would say politics in the broad sense.
G4174.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 22:28, Paul asserts before the Roman tribune that he possesses Roman citizenship by birth — a rare and prestigious fact that gives him legal protection. In Ephesians 2:12, Paul uses the same term to describe the spiritual and communal status of converted Gentiles: before Christ, they had no access to the chosen people of Israel, to its covenants, to its promises of salvation. It is a political image to express religious exclusion. Both usages highlight the notion of belonging: legal and physical in the case of Rome, spiritual and chosen in the case of Israel.
G4174.portee: This word reminds the believer that, through Christ, we have received a new status: we are no longer strangers to the people of God, but co-heirs of the promises and covenants (Ephesians 2:12-14). Understanding what Paul says about "citizenship" helps grasp the radical transformation that salvation brings: we move from exclusion to inclusion, from outside to inside the family of God. It is a call to gratitude and awareness of our new dignity in Christ.

sens: A city, a state, an organized political community
The homeland or country to which one belongs
The set of rights and duties of a citizen
A people united under a common authority
G4175.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a city or an organized political community — a state with its inhabitants, laws, and government. It conveys the idea of a place where citizens are bound together by common rules.
2. It can also refer to the homeland, the country, or the nation to which one belongs by birth or by heart. In Philippians 3:20, Paul states: "Our citizenship is in heaven" — he speaks of the true homeland of Christians, where Christ resides and where we hope to go.
3. The word can also evoke the status of citizenship itself, that is, the set of rights and duties that come with belonging to this city.
4. More broadly, it designates a community, a people, a group of men and women living together under a common authority.
G4175.origine: The word comes from the Greek politeuô (to act as a citizen, to live as a citizen), and shares its root with polis (the city) and politês (the citizen). It is a word that carries the idea of communal life and collective organization. In Hebrew, words like qiryah (city) or goy (nation, people) convey a similar idea.
G4175.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:20. Paul uses it to express a profound truth: while the Philippians are citizens of an important city in Macedonia (Philippi), Christians have a "city" that is far superior — the one that is in heaven. Paul plays on the contrast between earthly allegiance and heavenly allegiance. This word emphasizes that the Christian has a chosen homeland, a true country, beyond their current state.
G4175.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on their true belonging. Our true country is not primarily the territory where we were born; it is heaven, the kingdom of God. This puts our earthly loyalties into perspective and calls us to live as strangers and travelers on this earth, awaiting our final homeland with Christ.

sens: To live as a citizen of a political community
To lead one's life, to behave according to principles
To exercise moral or spiritual citizenship
G4176.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the existence and concrete life of the citizen in their city — it is about enjoying the rights and fulfilling the duties of one who belongs to an organized community. In this sense, it is to live as a full member of a city.
2. In the New Testament, this civic sense becomes spiritualized: "to conduct one's life" means to behave according to a moral code, a rule of life. Paul tells the Philippians (1:27): "Conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the Gospel," which means: behave, live your days, keeping in mind the honor of the Gospel.
3. For the Apostle Paul, this conduct takes on an even higher meaning: since Christians are citizens of heaven (Philippians 3:20), their "conduct" must reflect their belonging to this invisible kingdom. Acting as a citizen of heaven means living a life consistent with one's faith, as Paul shows in Acts 23:1 when he states he has "lived in good conscience before God."
G4176.origine: The word comes from politès (citizen), which is derived from polis (city). This is why it primarily means "to live as a citizen." The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses it rarely, always to speak of civil or political life. In the New Testament, the two occurrences in Paul reveal how the Gospel takes up ancient political language to express a spiritual reality: you are citizens, not of an earthly city, but of the kingdom of Christ.
G4176.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul. In Acts 23:1, Paul declares he has "conducted himself in all good conscience before God" before the Sanhedrin: this affirms that his entire life has been led according to the principles of his faith, in responsibility before God. In Philippians 1:27, the apostle urges believers to "conduct themselves in a manner worthy of the Gospel." This exhortation shows that for Paul, the Christian's "conduct" is a public testimony, a way to honor the Gospel. The word emphasizes the coherence between the profession of faith and daily behavior.
G4176.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that they are citizens of another world (Philippians 3:20) and that their ordinary life, concrete actions, and ethics are an expression of this heavenly citizenship. It is a reminder that faith is not confined to secret thoughts: it must "conduct itself," be shown, be embodied in every day. Paul encourages us to examine whether our way of living — at work, in family, in trials — truly honors the Gospel we profess.

sens: Inhabitant of a city or state, member of its political community
One who shares the same city or nationality as another person
G4177.detail:
1. A citizen is primarily one who belongs to a city or a country and is part of it. When Paul presents himself before the tribune in Jerusalem, he says, "I am a citizen of a city that is not insignificant" (Acts 21:39), meaning he enjoys the status of a citizen of Tarsus, a renowned city. In the parable of the prodigal son, the character "hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country" (Luke 15:15) — these inhabitants are the citizens of that distant country, those who enjoy rights and stability, unlike the foreigner that the prodigal son becomes.
2. In a second sense, it refers to the person with whom one shares this common belonging, the fellow citizen. When Jesus presents himself in Jerusalem to reign, the texts say that "his fellow citizens hated him" (Luke 19:14) — these are those who, like him, are of the same people and the same city. This is also the meaning of Hebrews 8:11: in the new covenant, "no one will teach his fellow citizen" because all will know the Lord, which emphasizes the unity of those who once shared the same religious instruction.
G4177.origine: The word comes from πόλις (polis), the city, just as σοφός (wise) comes from σοφία (wisdom). In Greek and Roman times, a citizen is not merely an inhabitant: it is one who enjoys particular rights and belongs to an organized political community. In the Septuagint, the Greek πολίτης often translates the Hebrew רֵעַ (friend, companion), showing that the citizen is one with whom one shares a common place, a civic or social brotherhood.
G4177.emploi: This word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Luke or in the epistles. In Luke 15:15 and Acts 21:39, it simply designates the inhabitant of a place, one who enjoys rights and stability there. In Luke 19:14 and Hebrews 8:11, it takes on the more precise meaning of fellow citizen, one who shares with us the same city or community. The Segond translates it sometimes as "citizen," sometimes as "inhabitant," sometimes as "fellow citizen," depending on the context: it is always the same idea of sharing a common belonging, but the emphasis is sometimes on the individual status (citizen of Tarsus), sometimes on the reciprocal relationship (my fellow citizen).
G4177.portee: This word reminds us that the believer, as an earthly citizen, belongs to a community. But the Pauline epistles also emphasize that the Christian is a "citizen of heaven" (Philippians 3:20): understanding πολίτης helps to grasp that citizenship is not just a legal matter, it is an identity, a belonging, a brotherhood. This is why, in the new covenant, the communion among brothers transcends old divisions: all, without exception, will know the Lord.

sens: Repeatedly, several times
In a rapid or habitual succession of events
With notable or excessive frequency
G4178.detail:
1. The word describes an action or event that occurs multiple times, without being continuous. In Matthew 17:15, the lunatic child "often falls into the fire, and often into the water": these falls happen regularly, not just once. It is the repetition that defines the moment.
2. It also emphasizes a habit or frequent return. In Acts 26:11, Paul says: "I often punished them in every synagogue" — the action has occurred many times, marking his past life. It is an established practice.
3. The word can carry a shade of insistence or exaggeration, especially when it signals repeated dangers or sufferings. In 2 Corinthians 11:26, Paul lists his perils: "Frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers" — the accumulation of risks is highlighted by this repeated enumeration.
G4178.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective « polys » which means « many, numerous ». By adding the suffix « -akis », it forms an adverb that emphasizes repetition: literally, « in a numerous manner » becomes « number of times ». It is a common word in Greek to express the frequency or iteration of an act.
G4178.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in Mark, Paul, and in the epistles. It describes repeated events: the lunatic son's fits, the punishments of the disciples by Paul, the perilous journeys of the apostle. In the epistles, it also expresses the frequency of a disposition: one has « often » experienced someone's zeal, one has « often » spoken of it. In Hebrews 9:25 and 10:11, it qualifies the repeated offering of the priests, in contrast to the unique sacrifice of Christ. The word remains neutral in itself, but it takes on color according to the context: the repetition of epileptic crises evokes distress, that of punishments violence, that of perils trial, and that of pastoral intercession vigilance.
G4178.portee: This word speaks to us about the reality of repeated struggles and sufferings in the life of the believer and the Church. It shows that certain trials — illness, temptation, doubt — often return and form a fabric of our existence, without necessarily being a sign of a failure of faith. At the same time, the frequency of acts of grace, of brotherly zeal, and of the faithful ministry of the apostle reminds us that perseverance and constancy shape the Christian life much more than unique heroic moments.

sens: Several times more, in quantity or intensity
Multiplied by a considerable whole number
Abundantly increased, beyond what was given
G4179.detail:
1. The word describes something that repeats or accumulates several times in succession: not just double, but much more. In Luke 18:30, Jesus promises that whoever has left house, brothers, or sisters for the Kingdom will "receive much more in this age."

2. It is a comparison in terms of multiplication: the benefit is not simply added, but multiplied. The word contains the idea of a thickness, a repeated depth (from the Greek πόλυς, « many », and λάσιος, « thick »), as if one were superimposing the same thickness multiple times.

3. In the context of the Kingdom, this term reveals divine generosity: what the disciple has left or sacrificed is returned to him with an abundance that exceeds all expectation and human calculation.
G4179.origine: The word comes from πόλυς (« many ») associated with the idea of multiplication: it carries within it the root λάσιος (« thick », « multiple »), which gives the image of an accumulated thickness. The Latin multiplex and the idea of « folds » (superimposed folds) reflect this notion of accumulation. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew שִׁבְעָתַיִם (« seven times »): the idea is always that of a repetition that adds to itself.
G4179.emploi: This word appears only once in the four Gospels, in Luke 18:30, in the promise made by Jesus to those who renounce everything for the Kingdom of God. Matthew 19:29 uses the cognate verb πολλαπλασίων with the same meaning. The usage is solemnly eschatological: it concerns divine retribution both in this age and in the age to come. The context shows that Jesus is not speaking of a literally multiplied material compensation, but of an incomparable spiritual and communal blessing.
G4179.portee: This word reminds Christians that God is never in debt to those who sacrifice for His Kingdom: what seems a loss in the eyes of the world is returned a hundredfold, not in terms of possessions, but in the richness of spiritual family (brothers, sisters, mothers) and in eternal life. It is a promise that invites radical trust and generosity without calculation.

sens: The act of speaking a lot, multiplying words
Discourse characterized by too many words, by verbosity
Prayer or speech where words are accumulated without depth
G4180.detail:
1. The word simply designates the act of speaking a lot, multiplying words. It is an accumulation of words, a certain prolixity of discourse (Matthew 6:7).
2. More precisely, it is a flaw: speaking too much, in a vain or hollow manner, without this flow of words adding anything substantial. In Matthew 6:7, Jesus criticizes those who pray "with many words," meaning they think that the length or quantity of words makes prayer more effective.
3. This abundance of words reflects a false understanding of prayer: believing that God listens more if one speaks longer. It is the error of the pagans who imagined that multiplying magical or religious formulas would ensure their requests were granted. Jesus' message: true prayer does not need this unnecessary flow.
G4180.origine: The Greek word πολυλογία is composed of « poly- » (many) and « logia » (word, speech, from logos). It literally means « many words ». The Greek Old Testament also speaks of numerous words (Proverbs 10:19), showing that this criticism of excessive talking is ancient in biblical wisdom: wisdom rather advises restraint and discretion in speech.
G4180.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 6:7. Jesus uses it to steer His disciples away from a prayer practice that He deems ineffective and erroneous. The « pagans » He criticizes are those who believe that the volume or quantity of words will impress or sway the gods. Jesus contrasts this with true prayer: one that comes from a sincere heart and does not seek to "make noise" before God. This critique fits within the teaching of the Sermon on the Mount, where He reminds that God knows the needs of His children before they ask (Matthew 6:8).
G4180.portee: This word from Jesus purifies our understanding of prayer. It frees us from the superstition that length or number of words makes us more "heard". It calls us to sincerity rather than appearance, to trust in God's listening rather than persuasion through rhetoric. For the Christian, this means that a brief prayer from the heart is better than an elaborate but empty discourse.

sens: in ancient times, before now
in several instances, gradually, in stages
in a fragmentary or partial manner
G4181.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes what happened in a distant past: "formerly" refers to the bygone era of the fathers and the prophets, before the coming of Christ. In Hebrews 1:1, it places the entire Old Testament in this past: "God, formerly, at many times and in many ways, spoke."
2. But "formerly" also expresses the idea of fragmented repetition: God did not speak just once, in a single voice. He addressed the fathers "many times," like successive steps, each one completing the previous one — a progressive revelation, built up gradually.
3. Finally, the word emphasizes the partial and incomplete nature of this ancient word: each prophet received only a part of the message, "in many different ways." This is an implicit contrast with the fullness of revelation in Jesus Christ in Hebrews 1:2.
G4181.origine: The word comes from the Greek "polus" (many) and "meros" (part, portion). The adverb "polumeros" literally denotes what is divided into many parts — a fragmented whole, composed of pieces. The image is that of a word that progresses in successive touches rather than an immediate and total revelation.
G4181.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 1:1. It opens the letter to the Hebrews by characterizing the way God spoke in the Old Testament: at many times, through various different prophets, in diverse forms (visions, dreams, audible words…). This adverb places the entire Old Testament under the sign of progression and fragmentation, in implicit opposition to what follows: the definitive and unique word of Jesus Christ.
G4181.portee: This word reminds the believer that divine revelation has been built progressively: each book, each prophet, each era of the Old Testament contributes a piece of the puzzle. It helps us to read the Old Testament not as a collection of disordered stories, but as a word that moves toward its fulfillment in Christ. It is also an invitation to patience: God speaks when and how it is right, and each step has its meaning.

sens: That presents a great diversity of forms, colors, or aspects
That is complex and rich due to the multiplicity of its elements
That manifests a multiple and nuanced wisdom
G4182.detail:
1. The word first describes something that offers a great variety of appearances: numerous and different colors, multiple shapes. It is the image of the colorful, the highly diverse on the surface. In Ephesians 3:10, Paul speaks of the "manifold wisdom of God" — not a simple and uniform wisdom, but a wisdom that manifests itself in a thousand different ways.
2. Beyond the visual aspect, the word evokes multiplicity and complexity: a richness that cannot be reduced to a single type or expression. The wisdom of God is not monotonous; it is rich in infinite nuances.
3. In this context, "infinitely varied" emphasizes how God unfolds His wisdom in extraordinarily diverse ways — in the history of salvation, in the plan of the Church, in the mystery long hidden but now revealed to the nations.
G4182.origine: The word is composed of "poly-" (many, numerous) and "poikilos" (varied, colorful). "Poikilos" evokes the image of fabrics or garments in multiple and contrasting colors. The basic idea is thus one of "great variety" or "extreme diversity."
G4182.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 3:10. Paul uses it to qualify the "wisdom" of God revealed through the Church to the heavenly powers. The context shows that this wisdom is not flat or predictable: it is rich, complex, multifaceted. It particularly manifests itself in the mystery of salvation granted also to the Gentiles, a plan that God had hidden during previous ages but which now unfolds with surprising depth.
G4182.portee: This word reminds us that the wisdom of God is never simply a matter of recipes or uniform answers. God acts with infinite richness and subtlety, adapting His plan to each circumstance, revealing always new facets of His nature and love. For the believer, this invites discovery of this diversity of divine grace in their own life and in the history of salvation.

sens: in large quantity or number
of considerable extent, duration, or intensity
numerous people (in plural)
a large number or the majority (noun)
comparatively more or greater
very, to a significant degree
G4183.detail:
1. The word designates what exists or presents itself in large quantity: "He taught them many things in parables" (Mark 4:2) means that there were a great number. "Many people from the country went up to Jerusalem before the Passover" (John 11:55) describes a large crowd.

2. It applies to qualities or states that are significant by their degree: "your reward will be great in heaven" (Luke 6:23) speaks of a considerable reward. "Great lamentation" (Matthew 2:18) evokes intense and manifest sorrow.

3. Used as a plural noun, it designates numerous people: "the Jews who had come from Jerusalem surrounded him, and brought against him many accusations" (Acts 25:7) shows that several Jews presented multiple accusations.

4. Substantivized, it means the majority or a large number: "He who gathered much had nothing left over" (2 Corinthians 8:15) speaks of one who had accumulated a great quantity.

5. Its comparative "more" or "greater" establishes a relationship between two quantities or magnitudes: in expressions like "more people," "more serious." 

6. Adverbially, it reinforces the intensity of an action or feeling: "many" then becomes a modifier indicating a high degree of a reality.
G4183.origine: The word πολύς comes from an Indo-European root denoting abundance and multiplication. In Hebrew, it primarily corresponds to רַב (rab), which expresses quantity, importance, and authority — the underlying image is that of what multiplies, extends, overflows. Its variants include the comparative πλείων (more) and the superlative πλεῖστος (the most), which follow the same logic of progressive increase.
G4183.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (341 occurrences). It appears in all the gospels to describe the crowds ("many followed him," Mark 5:24), teachings ("many parables," Mark 4:2), healings ("many sick," Mark 1:34), and material goods ("much money," Matthew 26:9). Paul uses it to speak of Christians ("many brothers"), trials ("many afflictions," 2 Corinthians 8:2), and blessings ("much grace"). Its meaning varies according to context: quantitative with countable nouns ("many people"), qualitative with abstracts ("great joy," "great noise"), and comparative with its forms πλείων ("more") and πλεῖστος ("the most"). The adjective can also be substantivized to designate "the many" or "the numerous" in opposition to the unique or the small number.
G4183.portee: This word anchors faith in the concrete of human experience: the crowds that follow Jesus, the miracles that multiply, the grace that abounds show that God works massively and visibly. "Many" also emphasizes that salvation and the Gospel are not reserved for an elite, but offered widely. At the same time, Jesus teaches that the narrow way that many find is opposed to the broad way (Matthew 7:13-14) — numerical abundance is not always a sign of truth. The word invites the reader to measure divine mercy by its vast reach.

sens: Deeply moved by the suffering of others and inclined to help
Who forgives and bears with kindness
Who acts with tenderness and pity towards the suffering
G4184.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one whose heart is touched to the depths by another's pain — a visceral emotion that naturally leads to helping. In James 5:11, God is described as "full of mercy" towards Job in his sufferings: this means that His compassion is complete and overflowing, not calculated or measured.
2. This mercy is not mere sentimental pity, but a disposition to forgive and bear with kindness the one who deserves punishment or who falters under the weight. It expresses the capacity to not punish one who could have been punished, and to accompany the weak.
3. The word speaks of a tenderness that acts: in James 5:11, the Lord's mercy is concretely manifested by giving Job a happy ending after his trials. It is a compassion that changes things.
G4184.origine: The Greek word is composed of πολύς ("many, abundant") and σπλάγχνον ("bowels, heart"). The bowels were considered in Hebrew thought as the seat of deep emotions, particularly mercy. Thus, πολύσπλαγχνος literally paints someone whose bowels are full of compassion, overflowing with pity. It is a hapax in the New Testament: this word appears only here, forged to express with intensity divine mercy.
G4184.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in James 5:11. The apostle James uses it to describe the Lord in His relationship to Job. After urging believers to patience in the face of trials, he invites them to recognize that God Himself is "full of mercy and compassion" — not a distant and unmerciful judge, but a father touched by the suffering of His children. This rare appearance shows that the word was deliberately chosen to emphasize the intensity and abundance of divine mercy.
G4184.portee: For the suffering believer, this word reminds that God is not indifferent to their pain. His mercy is not timid or reluctant, but "full," generous, overflowing. By naming God this way in the context of Job's trials, James teaches us that our trust can rest on God's inner tenderness, and that His compassion works for our good, even when we do not yet see the end He is preparing.

sens: That costs a lot of money, of great material value
Sumptuously adorned, luxuriously dressed
Precious, esteemed morally or spiritually
G4185.detail:
1. Refers to a material object that has a high cost and reflects its rarity or exceptional quality. The pure nard perfume poured by the woman in Bethany is described as being of great price, meaning it has a very high market value (Mark 14:3).

2. Also describes a garment or adornment that displays luxury through its richness, its costly ornaments. The apostle Paul warns against sumptuous clothing — these expensive garments that attract admiration by their cost (1 Timothy 2:9).

3. Figurative use: that which has great moral or spiritual value in the eyes of God, although it is invisible and without external ornament. A gentle and quiet spirit is of great price in God's sight, far more precious than any jewelry or expensive clothing (1 Peter 3:4).
G4185.origine: The word combines πολύς (many) and τέλος (completion, end, price to pay). The starting image is that of a completed expenditure, the price fully paid. It thus designates what requires a considerable expenditure, what has cost a lot. The Greek word often translates the Hebrew יָקָר (iqar, precious, honored) in the Old Testament, showing that the Hebrew Bible saw material and spiritual value as closely related realities.
G4185.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In the first two uses (Mark 14:3 and 1 Timothy 2:9), it qualifies material realities: a nard perfume and ornamental clothing. But Paul and Peter turn it by applying it to the spiritual and moral realm. In 1 Timothy 2:9, Paul contrasts expensive clothing with decent attire — to show that true Christian adornment is not what one buys. In 1 Peter 3:4, the word shifts: moral and spiritual purity becomes what is of value in God's eyes, more precious than any costly object. It is a clever diversion of luxury vocabulary for the service of the Gospel.
G4185.portee: This word invites the Christian to question value: what is truly precious? Material luxury dazzles and costs a lot, but it passes. Moral character — gentleness, inner peace, purity — is invisible and costs nothing in money, but God considers it infinitely precious. It is a word of freedom for those who do not possess much: your true dignity is not in what you wear.

sens: That costs a lot of money, that has a great market value
That is highly esteemed, deserving of respect and honor
That surpasses in excellence, more precious than anything else
G4186.detail:
1. The word describes a material object whose financial value is very high. The pearl in Matthew 13:46 and the pure nard perfume in John 12:3 are costly, sought-after goods that can only be obtained at the price of considerable effort or expense.
2. Beyond mere price, the word evokes what is venerated, respected, chosen for its rarity and superior quality. Such an object is worthy of honor and special attention.
3. The word takes on a spiritual significance when it compares tested faith to perishable gold: faith is "more precious" (1 Peter 1:7), meaning it surpasses in value all that exists on earth, even the most prestigious material things.
G4186.origine: The Greek word is formed from "polys" (many, numerous) and "timé" (price, value, honor). It literally evokes what has much value or much price. The word "timé" can mean both monetary price and the honor given to someone, which unites in Greek the notion of material wealth and that of esteem.
G4186.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to qualify material things or spiritual realities of exceptional value. In the parable of the kingdom (Matthew 13:46), a man sells everything to buy a pearl of great price: the word emphasizes that the pearl is worth every sacrificed penny. In John 12:3, the costly perfume that Mary pours on Jesus' feet is described as of great price, marking the generosity of the gesture. In 1 Peter 1:7, the word shifts towards moral and spiritual meaning: tested faith is compared to pure gold that is refined by fire, but it is "more precious" than that gold, for it has an eternal value that only perishable material lacks.
G4186.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize true values: what costs a lot is not always what is most precious, and vice versa. Faith, the Gospel, eternal life are of "great price" — they deserve that one sacrifices everything to obtain them, like the merchant in the parable. It is a call to reevaluate one's priorities and sacrifices in light of the Kingdom of God.

sens: In multiple ways, distinct modes or means
With diversity and variation in form or expression
Using different approaches according to circumstances
G4187.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of multiplicity and variety: not a single path, but several paths taken in turn. In Hebrews 1:1, God spoke to our fathers "in various ways" — sometimes through visions, sometimes through dreams, sometimes through direct words to the prophets — to communicate His message according to the needs and dispositions of each individual.
2. This diversity also implies a certain adaptation: not a uniform message delivered in a single way, but a flexible communication that takes on various forms. God did not speak once for all in a single manner; He multiplied the approaches to make Himself heard.
3. The term finally highlights the richness of the revelatory process: the multiplicity of ways does not weaken the message; it enriches it. It shows God's patience and pedagogy, adapting His teaching to the understanding of His people.
G4187.origine: The Greek word πολυτρόπως (polutropōs) is formed from πολύς (polús, much) and τρόπος (tropos, manner, turn, way). The basic image is that of "turning" or "multiplicity of turns": like an object that one would turn in every direction to look at it from various angles. The word belongs to the vocabulary of versatility and formal diversity, without a negative connotation of changeability or instability.
G4187.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 1:1, where it describes how God spoke to the fathers through the prophets. It fits within the context of the opening of the prologue of Hebrews, contrasting this ancient, fragmentary, and multiple communication with the ultimate revelation brought by the Son. The choice of this term emphasizes the progressive and diverse nature of the Old Testament: the prophecies, the laws, the stories, the wisdom — all the ways through which God addressed Israel before the incarnation.
G4187.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to recognize that God is never confined to a single form of communication. It teaches divine flexibility and God's infinite pedagogy: even in the Old Testament, God was already adapting His message, His signs, His actions to the understanding capacity of His people. For the believer, it is a lesson in humility: we must not confine God to our expectations of a single way of acting or speaking. It is also an invitation to honor the richness of Scripture, which presents God in a great variety of forms and faces.

sens: What one drinks, liquid intended to quench thirst
Figuratively, that which nourishes the soul or spirit, as drink nourishes the body
G4188.detail:
1. The word simply designates a drink, what one consumes. In 1 Corinthians 10:4, Paul speaks of the "spiritual drink" that the Israelites drank in the desert: the water from the rock that followed the people and which, according to Paul, prefigured Christ Himself.
2. Figuratively, the drink represents that which sustains the soul or spirit. In Hebrews 9:10, the "drinks" are among the legal prescriptions of the Old Covenant — foods, drinks, washings — which are "carnal ordinances," external practices intended to prepare hearts until the arrival of Christ.
G4188.origine: The word πόμα comes from the verb πίνω ("to drink"). It is a late form of the ancient Athenian Greek πῶμα. The word retains the basic idea of the verb: that which is absorbed by drinking. In the Greek Old Testament, the word translates the Hebrew שִׁקּוּי ("drink"), which has the same etymological family.
G4188.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 10:4, it designates the miraculous spiritual drink that God provides to His people in the desert — a supernatural water, symbol of Christ. In Hebrews 9:10, it appears in a list of legal observances of the Old Covenant, where it represents a ceremonial obligation rather than an ordinary drink. The context shifts: from a miraculous and prophetic drink to a legal practice that will pass away.
G4188.portee: For the Christian, these two uses remind us that God reveals Himself and nourishes His people through concrete signs. The rock from which water flows symbolizes Christ, who quenches the spiritual thirst of God's people. The enumeration in Hebrews invites us to understand that the external legal observances of the Old Covenant have given way to a transformed relationship in Christ.

sens: Malice, intention to do harm to someone
The sum of vices and evil acts
Disposition of the heart corrupted by sin
Spiritual power of evil at work in the world
G4189.detail:
1. Wickedness is primarily a malicious intention directed against others. Jesus knows the wickedness of the Pharisees who tempt Him (Matthew 22:18): they are driven by the desire to do Him harm.
2. The word also designates the concrete sum of evil acts and vices that spring from the corrupted heart. Mark 7:22 lists wickedness among thefts, covetousness, and slander: these are works of sin.
3. It expresses the deep corruption of the heart, the inner state of the sinner. The Pharisee is "full of extortion and wickedness" inwardly (Luke 11:39), although outwardly pure: his malice is inscribed in his very being.
4. In a broader spiritual perspective, wickedness appears as a hostile power of evil that fights against believers (Ephesians 6:12). It is not merely a personal flaw, but an organized spiritual force against God.
G4189.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective πονηρός (ponēros), which means "bad" and originally suggests the idea of what is worn out, tired, then what is useless or harmful. In ancient Hebrew, the word it translates (רַע, ra') expresses evil in all its forms, from physical evil to moral evil. The word family encompasses all vices and corruptions that emanate from a heart turned away from God.
G4189.emploi: The word πονηρία appears seven times in the New Testament, always to designate sin in terms of malice and corruption. It is used in the singular to describe the evil intention (Matthew 22:18, Luke 11:39), but also in the plural to enumerate wickedness as concrete acts and vices (Mark 7:22, Acts 3:26, Romans 1:29). Paul associates it with "malice" (κακία) to designate the totality of sin from which the believer must be purified (1 Corinthians 5:8). The word appears in lists of vices and in calls to conversion, showing that wickedness is one of the major sins from which man must turn away.
G4189.portee: Wickedness, in biblical language, is never a mere flaw or moral weakness: it is an active sin, a corruption of the heart that drives one to do harm. Recognizing one's own wickedness is to acknowledge one's complicity with evil and one's need for conversion. Understanding that evil also has an organized spiritual dimension (Ephesians 6:12) helps the Christian not to downplay the spiritual battle that is theirs and to arm themselves with prayer and faith to resist it.

sens: That which causes pain, suffering, labor
That which is of poor quality, worthless
That which is morally bad, contrary to God's justice and goodness
A wicked, immoral person, hostile to God
Satan, the enemy of God and source of evil
An envious or jealous gaze
G4190.detail:
1. Originally, the word designates that which tires, that which weighs down: a difficult situation, a trying time (Ephesians 5:16 speaks of "evil days," hard times to go through).

2. It qualifies that which is of poor quality or worthless: a bad fruit comes from a bad tree and cannot be good (Matthew 7:17).

3. It designates moral evil: evil thoughts that come from the heart defile a person (Mark 7:23), for the evil heart produces evil (Matthew 12:34-35).

4. Applied to people, it describes one who acts with malice: the wicked servant (Matthew 18:32), the evil man who refuses mercy.

5. Used in the singular "the evil" ("the wicked"), it refers to Satan himself, the adversary who opposes God and seeks to deceive believers: "deliver us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13).

6. The "evil eye" is the envious, jealous eye: one who looks with covetousness at what others possess (Matthew 20:15).
G4190.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to work, to toil." Originally, it designates that which causes hard work, fatigue — the idea of a burden that overwhelms. From there, it took on the broader meaning of "evil," "harmful." In Hebrew, it primarily translates the word רַע (ra'), which also carries this dual nuance: that which causes harm, that which is damaging, and that which is morally reprehensible.
G4190.emploi: The word appears 73 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew (25 occurrences) and in the epistles of John. It covers several contexts: sin and the corruption of the human heart (Mark 7:23: evil thoughts), the wickedness of people (1 Corinthians 5:13: remove the wicked from among you), the nature of moral evil (John 3:19: men preferred darkness because their works were evil), and especially Satan (Matthew 13:38-39: the evil one sows bad seeds). The word can also qualify difficult circumstances (Ephesians 5:16: redeem the time, for the days are evil) or an attitude of jealousy (Matthew 20:15: "Are you envious because I am good?").
G4190.portee: This word reminds the believer that evil is not abstract: it emanates from the human heart and from the prince of darkness who dominates it. It invites one to scrutinize their thoughts and intentions, knowing that the evil heart produces evil (Matthew 12:35). At the same time, recognizing evil as such — in the world, in others, in oneself — is the first step toward repentance and toward the protection that faith in Christ provides against the schemes of the Evil One.

sens: Hard work, labor
Fatigue and concern caused by intense effort
Physical or moral suffering, torment
Grief, sorrow
Consequence of suffering: torment, anguish
G4192.detail:
1. The word first designates hard work, laborious effort: in Colossians 4:13, Epaphras shows great "concern" (the same word) for the Christians, meaning a labor of love and devotion.
2. From this labor arises fatigue and worry: one who strives intensely feels a concern mixed with pain.
3. The word then shifts to physical and moral suffering: in Revelation 16:10-11, men tormented gnaw their tongues in pain because of the plagues that strike them.
4. It is emotional pain, grief: something that weighs on the heart and hurts.
5. Pain thus becomes the inevitable fruit of suffering endured: in Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away "every tear" and there will be no more pain in the new heaven, for "the former things have passed away." The word expresses this torment that accompanies the state of weakness and suffering of wounded creatures.
G4192.origine: The Greek word ponos comes from a root that evokes the effort and fatigue of physical work. In Hebrew, it often translates the word עָמָל (amal), which designates difficult and painful labor, particularly that mentioned in Psalm 90 as the consequence of sin. The word belongs to the same family as Greek verbs expressing "to work" and "to toil." It is a concrete word at its origin, which gradually enriches itself with an emotional and moral dimension.
G4192.emploi: The word πόνος appears only 4 times in the New Testament. In Colossians 4:13, it designates the laborious and devoted concern of Epaphras for the churches. Then, it takes on a darker meaning: in Revelation 16:10-11, it expresses the acute pain of men struck by eschatological plagues, that which accompanies perdition and refusal of repentance. Finally, in Revelation 21:4, it appears negatively in the promise of the new creation: there will be no more pain, for God himself will wipe away the tears of the redeemed. The nuance thus shifts from voluntary labor to involuntary suffering, from devotion to torment.
G4192.portee: This word reminds the Christian that life involves work and fatigue, whether through love like Epaphras, or through trial like those who suffer. But it also places this reality in hope: pain is not eternal. The promise of Revelation 21:4 invites the believer to hold on amid their pains, for God himself has promised to wipe away every tear and abolish suffering forever in the glorious presence of Christ.

sens: belonging to Pontus
coming from Pontus
inhabitant of Pontus
