G4193.detail: 1. The word designates that which belongs to the region of Pontus, an ancient province of Asia Minor (modern-day northern Turkey). In Acts 18:2, we encounter Aquila, described as "Aquila, born in Pontus" (Ποντικὸς) — it is an adjective that qualifies the geographical origin of a person, as one might say today "a Norman" or "an Alsatian." 2. By extension, the word can designate an inhabitant originating from Pontus, a person born in that region who retains that identity. 3. Figuratively, it is a marker of identity and provenance: the biblical text uses this detail to tell us who Aquila was, where he came from, and thus to help us situate him in history.
G4193.origine: The word comes from the proper name Pontus (Πόντος), which designated a historical region along the southern coast of the Black Sea. The adjective is formed simply by adding the suffix -ικός (-ikos), common in Greek to create adjectives of relation or belonging (like "Hellenic" for that which belongs to Greece). It is an ethnic or geographical adjective, which links a person or thing to its place of origin.
G4193.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:2, to qualify Aquila. He is a Jew native of Pontus who settled in Corinth. Its use is purely informative: the author of Acts mentions Aquila's geographical origin to specify his identity and life journey — he traveled from Pontus to Corinth. This mention also situates Aquila in a historical context: the Jews of the Diaspora, dispersed throughout all the provinces of the Roman Empire.
G4193.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel spread among Jews from all regions of the known world. Aquila, although native of a distant region, was led to meet Paul and become a key collaborator in the expansion of the Christian message. It is a testimony of how divine Providence gathers people from all backgrounds to accomplish His work.

sens: Roman governor of Judea who condemned Jesus to death
G4194.detail: 1. Pontius Pilate is the first name (praenomen) of the Roman governor who presided over the trial of Jesus and pronounced the sentence of crucifixion. In the New Testament, he is referred to by this first name or by his full name "Pontius Pilate" (Matthew 27:2), and sometimes simply by his family name. He governed Judea under the authority of Emperor Tiberius at the time of Jesus' condemnation (Luke 3:1). His role in the passion of Christ is recalled in Acts as an act of injustice committed against God's holy servant (Acts 4:27), and it is before him that Jesus made his beautiful confession (1 Timothy 6:13).
G4194.origine: Pontius is the Latin first name (praenomen) of the Roman governor. Historically, he is Pontius Pilatus, who governed Judea from approximately 26 to 36 AD. The Greek text of the New Testament designates him by this first name, a common usage among high-ranking Romans.
G4194.emploi: Pontius Pilate appears four times in the New Testament, always with his title of governor or in the context of the trial of Jesus. Luke places him historically under the reign of Tiberius Caesar (Luke 3:1). The Gospels report his role in the condemnation of Jesus (Matthew 27:2). The Acts of the Apostles depict him as an actor of injustice against Christ (Acts 4:27), and the epistle to Timothy mentions him as a witness to Jesus' confession before his death (1 Timothy 6:13).
G4194.portee: Pontius Pilate embodies in the New Testament one who has political power but yields to pressure to commit injustice. His example reminds Christians that even civil authority can submit to iniquity and that only God's justice prevails.

sens: region in the north of Asia Minor, on the southern coast of the Black Sea
G4195.detail: 1. Pontus is a historical region located on the southern shore of the Black Sea (called in Greek the "Black Sea"). It is a Roman province of Asia Minor, rich and prosperous. In Acts 2:9, inhabitants of Pontus are found in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost for the Jewish festival, indicating that there was a significant Jewish community in this region. In 1 Peter 1:1, Peter writes to believers scattered in Pontus and other nearby regions (Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia), indicating that the Gospel had spread to these places.
G4195.origine: The Greek name Pontos designates this region. It comes from the Greek word pontos which literally means "sea" — the region is named after the sea that borders it, the Black Sea ("Pont-Euxin" in Greek, meaning "Hospitable Sea"). It is an ancient way of naming territories by a dominant geographical feature.
G4195.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. First in Acts 2:9, where it is listed among the peoples and regions from which pilgrims gathered in Jerusalem during Pentecost. Then in 1 Peter 1:1, where Peter addresses his epistle to believers scattered in several regions of Asia Minor, including Pontus. These two occurrences show that Pontus was a center of Judaism and, after the coming of Christ, a field for the expansion of early Christianity.

sens: The chief magistrate of the island of Malta
He who received Paul and his companions after the shipwreck
G4196.detail: Publius is the governor or chief magistrate of the island of Malta, probably the Roman procurator who administered the island on behalf of Rome. He is the one who, upon learning of the arrival of Paul and his companions who were shipwrecked on the shore, generously welcomed them and hosted them for three days in his house (Acts 28:7). His Latin name reflects his status as a Roman citizen or at least a person of importance in local administration. He is distinguished by his hospitality towards foreign shipwrecked individuals and becomes the recipient of a miracle: Paul heals his father who was bedridden, afflicted with fever and dysentery, which enhanced the apostle's prestige among the inhabitants of Malta (Acts 28:8).
G4196.origine: Publius is a Latin name borne by several figures in the Roman Empire. It literally means "one who belongs to the people" (from the Latin populus, people). It is one of the three most common Roman first names. In the New Testament, this name appears here to identify a high-ranking Roman magistrate, reflecting Luke's historical accuracy and attention to detail in his account in Acts.
G4196.emploi: Publius appears twice in the New Testament, exclusively in chapter 28 of the Acts of the Apostles, during Paul's shipwreck on his way to Rome. He is presented as the "chief person of the island" (Acts 28:7), indicating his official status and administrative authority. His welcome of the shipwrecked individuals shows the generosity of local authorities and opens the door for Paul's ministry in Malta. The miracle of the healing of his father (Acts 28:8) becomes the starting point for a series of healings that mark Paul's visit to Malta and validate his apostolic authority among the inhabitants.
G4196.portee: The figure of Publius illustrates how God uses seemingly negative circumstances—a shipwreck—to accomplish His purposes. The hospitality of this Roman magistrate towards foreign prisoners and shipwrecked individuals reveals a humanity that faith can transform into an opportunity for testimony. The miracle of Publius' father demonstrates the power of the Gospel operating through the hands of the apostle, with concrete and visible effects that even touch powerful figures.

sens: the journey one takes from one place to another
path, walk, progression (in terms of movements or activities)
G4197.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a true journey, a physical trip on a road. In Luke 13:22, Jesus "was on His way to Jerusalem": He was actually walking, from town to town, to reach His destination.
2. The word can also evoke movement, the action of setting out or going. In James 1:11, applied to the rich who "will fade away in their pursuits", the word suggests a walk, an activity: the rich disappear like the withered flower, in full movement, in the very course of their business.
G4197.origine: The word comes from the verb πορεύω (poreuō), which means "to go, to walk, to journey". Poreia thus designates the journey itself, the action of walking. The family of the word evokes the idea of movement and progression. In Hebrew, the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) often translates the expression הֲלִיכָה (halikah) with this word, which carries the same meaning of "walk, journey."
G4197.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 13:22, it describes the concrete journey of Jesus: He travels through towns and villages teaching, making His way to Jerusalem — a real path, step by step. In James 1:11, the context changes: the word takes on a figurative hue, describing not a geographical journey but the course of the rich man's life, his pursuits, his activity — a "walk" that will vanish like the flower withers.
G4197.portee: This word reminds us that the life of a disciple is not static: it is a road to be traveled, a path with Jesus. It also invites us to measure the precariousness of riches: the rich man runs after his business, but all of this passes away. For the Christian, the question remains: where are you headed?

sens: to move from one place to another
to leave, to depart
to head towards, to go somewhere
to progress in a direction or action
to follow someone, to be a disciple
to walk in a moral or spiritual way
G4198.detail:
1. The simplest meaning is that of physical movement: to move, to go from one place to another. Jesus tells his disciples: "Go show yourselves to the priests" (Luke 17:14), meaning go to their place.
2. To leave, to distance oneself from a place or someone, as when Jesus says to the woman: "go in peace" (Luke 8:48), which means "be free to depart."
3. To intentionally head towards a place or person: "I am going to Jerusalem" (Acts 20:22), "Judas went to the chief priests" (Matthew 26:14).
4. To advance, to progress in an action or endeavor: to continue on one's path despite obstacles, like Paul who "goes" to Jerusalem despite the warnings of the Spirit.
5. In a figurative sense, to follow someone, to be their disciple or supporter, for example, "to go after someone."
6. To walk spiritually: to live according to a moral principle or law, as when the Bible speaks of going "in peace" or walking "according to the law."
G4198.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of passage or crossing (πόρος means ford or passage). In Hebrew, it regularly translates the verb הלךְ (halak), which is the ordinary word for walking and going. This Hebrew verb is used both literally (physically walking) and figuratively (living according to a moral path). The Greek πορεύω retains this dual dimension: physical movement and spiritual journey.
G4198.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament: about 146 occurrences. It appears in all the Gospels and in Acts, where the apostles are constantly moving to proclaim the Gospel. Matthew often uses it for the movements of disciples or crowds. Luke uses it in a particular way: not only for movements but also to express the spiritual journey ("go in peace"). In Acts, it describes missionary travels. The context changes the meaning: "to go" can be a simple movement (Matthew 2:8), an action commanded by God (Luke 17:14), or a personal commitment (Judas going to the priests). Paul also uses this verb to describe his journey to Jerusalem, fraught with challenges and dangers.
G4198.portee: This verb invites the reader to meditate on the movement of faith: to go means to obey, to advance despite uncertainty, to head towards God or to stray from Him. When Jesus says "go in peace," He both frees and sends. When Paul "goes" to Jerusalem knowing the sufferings that await him, he demonstrates profound obedience. The word reminds us that the Christian life is not static: it is a path, a walk, a response to the call to set out with God.

sens: To destroy, to ravage a city or place
To ruin, to annihilate an institution or community
To pursue and mistreat people for their beliefs
G4199.detail:
1. In the most brutal sense, the word describes the action of destroying or ravaging a physical place, like an army that sacks a city. It is a violent word that paints the image of devastation.

2. Transferred to the spiritual and social domain, it applies to the destruction of an institution or community: this is exactly what Paul says about himself in Galatians 1:13, when he acknowledges that he "was ravaging the Church of God," meaning he was attempting to annihilate it by organizing arrests and sowing terror among believers.

3. The concrete meaning then sharpens into that of persecution: to pursue someone relentlessly and maliciously to punish or eliminate them because of their beliefs. In Acts 9:21, the verb "persecuted" describes Paul's systematic action against those who invoked the name of Jesus in Jerusalem.
G4199.origine: The word πορθέω is an ancient and poetic form of the verb πέρθω (perthō), which means "to devastate" or "to destroy." It is a verb of Indo-European origin that depicts a violent and destructive action. The family of the word is small in biblical Greek, but it is very present in classical poetry. It is only in Paul, who re-describes his own past, that the word takes on this specific sense of ecclesiastical persecution.
G4199.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Pauline texts, and always in reference to the period when Paul himself was persecuting Christians before his conversion. In Acts 9:21, this is what the disciples of Damascus heard about him: that he was persecuting believers in Jerusalem. In Galatians 1:13, Paul himself testifies forcefully: he "was ravaging" the Church, organizing arrests. In Galatians 1:23, he adds that he "was trying" to destroy the faith he now proclaims. The word therefore always carries the mark of destructive and systematic zeal, although Paul acknowledges that it was a mistake driven by ignorance.
G4199.portee: This word reminds the reader of the historical reality of ancient persecution and its violence: Paul was not a lukewarm adversary, but an active agent of the Church's destruction. This magnifies the grace of God who stopped Paul on the road to Damascus and made him the most fruitful apostle. For the Christian, it is an invitation to recognize that even the worst persecutors can be transformed by an encounter with Christ, and that no one should despair of divine forgiveness.
